There is no load locally, so an autoscaled instance reports its compute capacity at the configured minimum. An incremental schedule (at most one backup every 4 hours, else `INVALID_ARGUMENT`; this supersedes the backup schedules row's refusal) takes chains: a full backup, then up to 13 incremental ones sharing `incremental_backup_chain_id` and the full backup's `oldest_version_time`; a new chain starts when the chain is full, its full backup is 28 days old, its newest backup is deleted, or the schedule changes. `freeable_size_bytes` is the newest backup's own growth and 0 for older ones; restoring or copying any backup of a chain works, and deleting or expiring one never breaks another (each local backup keeps a whole copy). Unit tests: `TestEditionsAndAutoscaling`, `TestIncrementalSchedulesNeedEnterprise`, `TestIncrementalChains`, `TestCreateInstancePartitionNeedsEnterprisePlus`. The messages are CloudBurrow's |

**Fifteen Bigtable RPCs would crash the emulator**, so CloudBurrow answers them itself (#1206):
the backup methods, the schema bundle methods, `UndeleteTable` (served since #1511) and the change stream reads (served since #1523).
`bttest` embeds a nil server for them, so a call panicked it: measured before #1206, the client saw
`UNAVAILABLE` "error reading from server: EOF", the pod restarted, and every table was lost. The
Bigtable pod now runs `cloudburrow-storage bigtable-front` (`internal/bigtablefront`) before the
emulator, which listens on the pod's loopback alone: it serves those fifteen and
passes every other call through, each message undecoded but the writes to a table with a change stream, which it decodes to log them.

**Bigtable and Spanner are in-memory; Datastore and Firestore keep their data in persistent mode.**
CloudBurrow provisions no volume for the two, and `status` lists them as never surviving a
restart, whatever `--mode` says. Datastore and Firestore have a volume in persistent mode, and
`status` says they survive a restart then (how, below). Measured 2026-10-16 across a whole-instance
restart, before Firestore kept its documents (#1615): on `up --mode persistent --services datastore,firestore,bigtable`, an entity, a Firestore
document and a Bigtable table were written with the official Go clients; after `cloudburrow stop`
and the same `up`, the entity read back, the document was `NOT_FOUND` and the table list was empty.

For Spanner this is now **measured rather than quoted**: `TestSpannerStateDoesNotSurviveARestart`
writes a row, restarts the pod, waits for the endpoint to come back, and reads —

```
after the restart the data is gone: spanner: code = "NotFound",
desc = "Instance not found: projects/.../instances/cb-durab"
```

The test fails rather than passes if the endpoint does not return, because an unreachable
address is not evidence about durability. It is on CI's [retry-once list](#retried-once), so this
evidence tolerates one retry.

**What the Spanner, Bigtable and Firestore fronts keep lives as long as the emulator's data (#1514).**
Each front keeps what its emulator does not: Spanner's backups and their rows, backup schedules,
database roles, drop protection, instance updates, custom instance configurations, partition
updates, IAM policies and operations; Bigtable's instances, clusters, app profiles, memory layers,
backups and snapshots with their cells, the tables kept for `UndeleteTable`, authorized, logical
and materialized views, schema bundles and IAM policies; Firestore's databases, indexes, field
overrides, backup schedules, backups with their documents, and operations. None of it is in the
front's memory alone: it is in a state directory on an **emptyDir of the pod, limited to 1 GiB**
(`internal/frontstate`), the records in one file replaced whole and each data copy in a file of
its own, written as the call that made it returns. So a restart of the front's container alone,
the emulator still running, loses none of it, and a restart of the pod loses it together with the
emulator's data, as the Pub/Sub (#898) and BigQuery (#1115) fronts' state does: none of it
survives `stop` and `up`, and none of it is in a `state save` archive. Firestore's is the
exception since #1615: its directory is the pod's PersistentVolumeClaim in persistent mode, with
the emulator's exported documents beside it, so its databases, indexes, schedules and backups
survive `stop` and `up` with the documents (next paragraphs but one). A pod whose copies grow past
the limit is evicted by the kubelet, and starts empty. `TestSpannerFrontRestartKeepsItsState`,
`TestBigtableFrontRestartKeepsItsState` and `TestFirestoreFrontRestartKeepsItsState` make each kind
of resource with the official clients, restart the front's container alone, and read them back:
a Spanner backup is restored into a database with its rows, a Bigtable backup into a table and a
deleted table is undeleted, each with its cells, and a Firestore backup is restored with its
documents. **`reset` clears it** (`TestResetClearsTheFrontsState`): `service=spanner`, `bigtable` and
`firestore` forget what each front keeps, and Bigtable's also drops the tables of the instances it
forgets; the Spanner emulator's instances and databases and the Firestore emulator's documents are
not reset, as before.

**Datastore keeps its data in persistent mode, measured (#307).** In persistent mode the
emulator's on-disk store is on a PersistentVolumeClaim, and the emulator's JVM is the container's
main process. The Cloud SDK emulator writes its whole store when it shuts down cleanly, and, while it has
changes, every 30 seconds (a fixed delay of its own, which no flag sets; measured #1611), and both
`gcloud beta emulators datastore start` and the `cloud_datastore_emulator` script run the JVM as
a child that never receives the pod's SIGTERM, so under the wrapper an entity written before a
pod restart was lost. In ephemeral mode it runs through the wrapper with `--no-store-on-disk`,
as it always did. The emulator loads its store when it starts, and a deleted pod's replacement,
which the ReplicaSet starts at once on the same volume, could load it before the old JVM had
even been signalled to save: with the call front in the pod (#1288) the entity written last was
lost in three runs of three (#1307). So the running JVM holds an exclusive `flock` on
`/data/datastore.lock` on the volume, and the next pod's emulator waits for it (its log says
`waiting for the previous emulator to save /data/datastore`) until the old one has saved and
exited; measured, five of nine pod restarts waited, and every one kept its data.
`TestDatastoreSurvivesAPodRestart` writes an entity with the Go client,
deletes the pod, and reads every entity written so far back from the new one, three times over.
An emulator that is killed rather than stopped (a full heap, node loss) loses what was written
since its last save, up to about 30 seconds (next paragraph). CI's restart probe reads a probe entity after `stop` and `up` in persistent mode, and
finds none after `up --mode ephemeral` (`TestDatastoreAcrossRestart`). Both tests are on CI's
[retry-once list](#retried-once), so this evidence tolerates one retry. `status` reports `volume` for Datastore and Firestore, and for every
other service, only in persistent mode. That Bigtable loses its data is measured
above (2026-10-16), not in CI.

**Firestore keeps its documents in persistent mode, measured (#1615).** The emulator holds
documents in memory alone, but exports a database's documents to a directory of its own
(`POST /emulator/v1/projects/{p}:export`, one database a call) and imports such an export into a
running emulator (`:import`, given the export's `overall_export_metadata` file); this emulator
(`cloud-firestore-emulator` of the pinned Cloud SDK image) also takes `--import-data` and
`--export-on-exit`, but those name one database's export, and the exit export needs a clean
shutdown. So the call front in the Firestore pod, which sees every call, keeps them
(`internal/firestoreadmin/documents.go`): every **30 seconds** in which a call that may write went
through it (Datastore's save interval), it exports every database it knows of (every database a
call named, and the Admin API's) into a new generation directory, then replaces a manifest naming
each export whole and removes the older generation, so a crash during an export leaves the last
one. When the pod stops it exports what was written since, and the emulator's container, whose
JVM ignores `SIGTERM`, waits for it (at most 10 seconds) before it kills the JVM; when the kind
node stops (`cloudburrow stop`), every process gets `SIGTERM` at once, and the same wait holds the
JVM. Each time the emulator starts (the pod's start, and every restart of its container, which
the front notices by a sentinel document of its own, in a project no call names, going missing)
the front imports the manifest's exports before it lets any documents or Admin API call through.
The directory is on the pod's volume, shared by both containers, which run as the same user: a
PersistentVolumeClaim in persistent mode, holding the Admin API's state beside it, so documents,
databases and backups survive `stop` and `up` together; a deleted pod's replacement waits on a
`flock` the old front holds until its last export, as Datastore's does (#1307). In **ephemeral
mode** the directory is the pod's emptyDir: the documents survive an exit of the emulator alone
(the table below), and go with the pod; `stop` and `up` restart the kind node, which keeps the
pod and its emptyDir, so a starting front discards the exports of the one before it
(`--firestore-documents-fresh`), and they live for the instance's life only, as before;
the periodic export is the same, and costs nothing while nothing writes. **Cost:** an export
writes every document of every database, at most once each 30 seconds and only while calls write,
so an idle emulator costs nothing; a handful of databases with a few documents each exported in
well under a second, and 100,000 documents of about 1 KB in one database in 1.35 seconds, 105 MB
on the volume, with their import on start 2.1 seconds (measured, #1615, `--emulator-heap-mib`
1024, which holds about 300,000 such documents). **A clean `stop`** first asks the front to
export what was written since its last export, through `up`'s tunnel, bounded by
`--shutdown-timeout` alone (2.1 seconds at 100,000 documents, and `stop` says so: "exported the
Firestore documents in …"), so every write that reached Firestore before `stop` is kept, whatever
the number of documents. The pod's own export as it stops, which also covers a deleted pod, is
bounded at 8 seconds (1.4 seconds at 100,000 documents; about 600,000 such documents fit in it),
and the kind node's stop gives its containers 10 seconds: a pod in the cluster that writes after
`stop`'s export, with more documents than fit in 8 seconds (a heap well over 2 GiB), loses what
it wrote since the last export, as on a crash; when `stop`'s export fails, `stop` prints a warning
naming that. `TestFirestoreSurvivesAPodRestart` writes to `(default)` and to a named database, deletes the
pod and reads every document back, twice over, and in ephemeral mode finds the last write gone;
CI's restart probe reads a probe document in each database, and the named database through the
Admin API, which `TestFirestoreRestartSetup` writes alone just before `stop` (#1636), after `stop` and `up` in persistent mode, and finds none after `up --mode ephemeral`
(`TestFirestoreAcrossRestart`). A call that may write (every Firestore call but the reads, and
every Admin API call but `Get` and `List`) is counted when it starts and when it ends, so one
still running during an export is exported by the next; a gRPC call is counted at each response
message too, which the emulator sends once the write it answers is committed, so a write in the
middle of a long `Write` stream is exported within the interval, not only when the stream ends.

**What a Firestore or Datastore emulator's exit loses (#1611).** Since #1603 each Java emulator's
heap is bounded (`--emulator-heap-mib`, 1024 MiB by default, [configuration.md](configuration.md#settings))
and the JVM exits at once when it is full (`-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError`, which runs no shutdown
hook, so nothing is saved), and the kubelet restarts the emulator's container alone, in seconds;
the front's container and its emptyDir are not touched. Measured by ending the JVM with `SIGKILL`
from the kind node, which is what that exit is to the emulator, through the official clients:

| | `--mode persistent` | `--mode ephemeral` |
|---|---|---|
| Firestore documents, in every database | Kept up to the front's last export, every 30 seconds while calls write; what was written since is lost (#1615) | The same: the export is on the pod's emptyDir |
| Firestore databases, indexes, field overrides, backup schedules, backups (with their documents), operations | Kept: the front's, on the pod's emptyDir | Kept |
| Firestore listeners | The official client's listener reconnects by itself: it may first be told its document no longer exists, then sees later writes | The same |
| Datastore entities | Kept up to the emulator's last save, about every 30 seconds; what was written since is lost | **Lost**: nothing is on disk |

A Firestore backup is still a way back: a schedule's backup outlives the emulator, and
`RestoreDatabase` makes a database with its documents. The emulator has no persistence of its own
(`gcloud`'s `--export-on-exit` needs a clean shutdown, which this exit is not); the front's
exports (#1615, above) are what bring the documents back. The bound is sized for real data rather than for the soak: 100,000 documents of about
1 KB held 330 MiB of Firestore's heap, and the 512 MiB of #1603 filled before a second 100,000 were in,
and the emulator exited, losing all of them; Datastore's 100,000 entities held 175 MiB, and 410 MiB while it wrote
its 110 MB store to disk, which needs 2.3 times the live heap. 1024 MiB holds about 300,000 such
Firestore documents and 240,000 Datastore entities. A persistent Datastore store too large for the
heap fills it at each save, so the emulator exits, loads the last save, and loses every 30 seconds'
writes; raise the bound, or set it to `0`. `TestFirestoreAfterTheEmulatorIsKilled` and
`TestDatastoreAfterTheEmulatorIsKilled` kill each emulator's JVM and read back what is kept, and
find what is lost gone, in either mode; Firestore's waits out an export interval first, and
logs whether a document written just before the kill came back.

**Firestore compacts its emulator's versions before the heap fills (#1969).** The Firestore
emulator keeps every version of every document in its heap for as long as it runs: overwriting 8
documents of 10 KB about 100,000 times filled the default 1 GiB heap, the JVM exited, and up to 30
seconds of writes (since the front's last export) were lost. The emulator's JVM now logs its
collections to the pod's shared volume (`-Xlog:gc,gc+init`), and the front reads that log four
times a second. Once a full collection leaves half the heap in use (or any collection 80%), the
front compacts: it closes the gate every documents call passes (new calls wait, as they do while
the documents are imported, and are not refused), lets the calls already in the emulator finish
for up to 5 seconds, ends the `Listen` and `Write` streams at once and any call still running after
that, with `UNAVAILABLE` and a `RetryInfo`, exports the documents, and has the emulator's
container restart the JVM (the emulator's own reset of a database's documents keeps their
versions, measured: a 160 MiB heap holding 6,000 versions of a 10 KB document still exhausted
itself on 9,000 more after it). The new JVM is given the export, as after any restart, and the gate
opens: about 1.2 seconds in all, measured with a 256 MiB heap. A call it ended was never answered,
and every answered write is in the export, so no acknowledged write is lost; a failed export, or
a container that does not take the restart, leaves the emulator as it was. The front's own calls to the emulator pass the same gate: the Admin API's reads and writes of documents (exports and imports, backups, restores and clones, bulk deletes, the `Write` streams, WebChannels and pipelines it passes on) and its clearing of a database in a purge wait while a compaction runs, and one already in the emulator is let finish before the export (unit `TestTheFrontsOwnWritesPassTheGate`), so none lands in the JVM that is about to restart. The cost is the
versions: the emulator holds none from before the compaction, so the database's
`earliest_version_time` moves to it, and a read at an earlier `read_time`, an export at an earlier
`snapshot_time` or a clone of an earlier minute is refused `FAILED_PRECONDITION`, even within the
hour or seven days Google would keep. Google keeps versions for the retention period whatever is
written; this is where CloudBurrow keeps fewer, and only for a write-heavy database. A heap sized
for the workload (`--emulator-heap-mib`) makes compactions rarer; if the documents alone, as
exported, take a quarter of the heap, the front logs that the heap should be raised and compacts
at most every 5 minutes. `TestFirestoreCompactsItsVersionsBeforeTheHeapFills`, through the
official Go client against `--emulator-heap-mib 256`: 53,694 writes of 10 KB to 8 documents (twice
the heap) at about 1,100 to 2,500 a second, with a small ledger document every 50; the front
compacted 4 times, the emulator's container never restarted nor logged an `OutOfMemoryError`,
every document held its last answered write and all 1,071 ledger documents were there, a listener
open throughout reconnected by itself and saw the last write, and a read at a time before the
compaction (within the hour) was `FAILED_PRECONDITION`, with `earliest_version_time` past it. Unit
`TestACompactionLosesNoAcknowledgedWrite` and `TestHeapWatchReadsFullCollections` cover the gate,
the ended streams and the log; the first injects the orderings a loaded run can take between the
export and the import (the run loop's check of the emulator in between, an old JVM still answering
after its restart was asked for, a call held at the gate past its wait), each of which lost
acknowledged writes before #2018.

### Firestore with MongoDB compatibility (#1703)

Google's Firestore with MongoDB compatibility, an Enterprise edition feature, is served by the
Firestore pod's call front itself, on a second port of the Firestore Service: the MongoDB wire
protocol, tunnelled to `--port-firestore-mongodb` (default `9026`) and exported by `cloudburrow env`
as `CLOUDBURROW_FIRESTORE_MONGODB_ENDPOINT`. It is CloudBurrow's own server: Google publishes no
emulator of it. The pages followed, re-read 2026-11-17: [overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/overview),
[connect](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/connect),
[behavior differences](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/behavior-differences),
[supported features 8.0](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/supported-features-80),
[data types](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/supported-data-types-drivers)
and [quotas](https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/quotas).

| Feature | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Connection and handshake: the connection string Google documents, `mongodb://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT/DATABASE_ID?loadBalanced=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&tls=true&retryWrites=false`, in load-balanced mode (`hello` with a `serviceId`), over TLS only; `ping`, `buildInfo`, `endSessions` | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`, through the official MongoDB Go driver (`go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2` v2.10.0, Go is 2.x in Google's driver table). The host is this instance's endpoint, not `UID.LOCATION.firestore.goog:443`. TLS only, as Google requires ("Drivers must connect with SSL enabled", #1738): `up` makes the instance's own CA (ECDSA P-256, ten years) and a 180-day server certificate for the loopback and the Firestore Service's names, issued again with less than 30 days left; the front serves TLS 1.2+. `cloudburrow env` exports the CA as `CLOUDBURROW_FIRESTORE_MONGODB_CA_FILE`, which a client names with `tlsCAFile=` (the console's connection strings carry it). A cleartext client and one that does not trust the CA are refused (tested). |
| Authentication: SCRAM-SHA-256 with the Admin API's user credentials, the user being the credentials' ID and the authentication database the database's ID; a connection is then limited to that one database, as Google's are | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`: the password `CreateUserCreds` returned authenticates; a wrong password, an unknown user and disabled credentials are refused `AuthenticationFailed` (18); after `ResetUserPassword` the old password is refused and the new one authenticates; an unauthenticated `find` is `Unauthorized` (13). Only an Enterprise edition database's credentials authenticate. A SCRAM user then needs, for each command, the permissions Google's IAM page lists for it in the roles granted to its credentials' principal, `principal://firestore.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/name/databases/DATABASE_ID/userCreds/USERNAME` ("A new user credential has no permissions by default", #1738): `TestFirestoreMongoDBIAMUserCreds`, with the official Resource Manager client, signs in with no role and is refused a read `Unauthorized` (13), reads with `roles/datastore.viewer` and is refused a write, and writes with `roles/datastore.user`. Google's documented binding carries a condition naming the database (`--condition='expression=resource.name == "projects/PROJECT_NAME/databases/DATABASE_ID"'`), and it is honoured (#1742, `TestFirestoreMongoDBIAMConditions`, the official Resource Manager client): with the condition naming the user's database the user writes, naming another it is refused `Unauthorized` (13); a `request.time` condition in the past grants nothing and one in the future grants the role. A conditional binding is evaluated at each command with the attributes Google's "Resource attributes for IAM Conditions" gives a Firestore database: `resource.service` `firestore.googleapis.com`, `resource.type` `firestore.googleapis.com/Database`, `resource.name` `projects/PROJECT_ID/databases/DATABASE_ID`, and `request.time`. A conditional role counts for `listDatabases` before a database is chosen where it holds for one of the project's databases. A custom role is evaluated by the permissions it holds (#1743). |
| Authentication with an access token: `PLAIN` (user `access_token`, from `$external`) and `MONGODB-OIDC`, and the IAM role check | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDBIAMToken` (#1738): only a live access token this instance minted signs in (checked by its SHA-256 against the instance's log of minted tokens, as Memorystore's IAM auth does), here minted through the official IAM Credentials client; a made-up one is `AuthenticationFailed` (18). Each command needs the permissions Google's IAM page lists for it in the principal's roles on the database's project (`roles/owner`, `editor`, `viewer`, `datastore.owner`, `datastore.user`, `datastore.viewer`, `datastore.indexAdmin`), granted through the official Resource Manager client: `roles/datastore.user` reads and writes, `roles/datastore.viewer` reads and is refused a write `Unauthorized` (13), no role is refused a read, `MONGODB-OIDC` signs in the same way, and a role taken back refuses the next command. `listDatabases` before a token connection has chosen its database needs `datastore.databases.getMetadata` on some project and lists the Enterprise databases of the projects that grant it (`TestFirestoreMongoDBIAMUserCreds`). The host pushes the tokens and roles to the front every 5 s when they change, and as each token is minted. A custom role is evaluated by the permissions it holds (#1743, `TestFirestoreMongoDBIAMCustomRole`, the IAM custom roles section). Roles on the database rather than its project are not served. |
| `insert`, `find` (filter, sort, skip, limit, projection, `batchSize`), `getMore`, `killCursors`, `count`, `distinct`, `update` (the update operators, replacements, `multi`, `upsert`), `delete`, `findAndModify` | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`: `InsertMany`, a duplicate `_id` refused `DuplicateKey` (11000), `Find` with a filter, a descending sort, a limit and a projection, a cursor over five documents two at a time and one closed early, `FindOne` by string and ObjectId `_id`, `CountDocuments`, `EstimatedDocumentCount`, `Distinct`, `UpdateOne` (`$set`, `$inc`, `$push`), `UpdateMany`, an upsert, `FindOneAndUpdate` returning the new document, `DeleteOne` and `DeleteMany`. The fields Google lists as unsupported for each command are refused `CommandNotSupported` (115). The query operators are evaluated by the front over the collection's documents, in MongoDB's comparison order; `$where`, `$jsonSchema`, `$comment` and the bitwise query operators are refused `BadValue`, as Google does not support them. Retryable writes are not supported, as on Google: the connection string sets `retryWrites=false`. |
| `aggregate` | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`: `$match`, `$group` (`$sum` of a field and a count) and `$sort`; `CountDocuments` is an aggregate too. Also served: `$project`, `$addFields`/`$set`, `$unset`, `$skip`, `$limit`, `$count`, `$unwind`, `$replaceRoot`/`$replaceWith`, `$sortByCount`, `$facet`, `$lookup` with `localField`/`foreignField`, and the arithmetic, comparison, boolean, conditional, string, array and conversion expressions Google lists, unit-tested alone. `$out` and `$merge` are refused, as Google does not support them (tested), and a pipeline is limited to 250 stages. `$lookup` with a pipeline and collection-less aggregations are the next rows. |
| `createIndexes`, `listIndexes`, `dropIndexes` | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`: a unique index on one field is created (`isbn_1`), refuses a duplicate key, is listed by the driver and by the Admin API's `ListIndexes` as a `MONGODB_COMPATIBLE_API` index. Indexes are READY at once and change no result, as every index here; a unique one is enforced on writes. Wildcard indexes are refused, as on Google; Google's limits of 1000 indexes a database and 100 fields an index are enforced. |
| Documents are the database's Firestore documents | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`: the official Firestore Go client reads what the driver wrote, an `int32` as `BSONInt32` and a `$inc` result, and the driver reads a document the Firestore client wrote, its document ID as its `_id`. A collection is a root collection and a string `_id` that is a valid document ID is the document ID; Google does not document how another `_id` names its document, so CloudBurrow names it `~o:` and the ObjectId's hex, `~i:`, `~l:` or `~d:` and the number, or `~v:` and the value's BSON in base64url (a string `_id` that is not a valid document ID, or starts with `~`, is `~s:` and its base64url). The BSON types are Firestore values as Google's mapping table documents (`__int__`, `__oid__`, `__regex__` and the rest); for them the Firestore emulator runs as an Enterprise edition emulator, and the front keeps a Standard edition database to Standard's values (next row). A Firestore map keeps no field order, so a document's fields read back in name order, `_id` first. Google's naming and document limits are enforced: `__.*__` names, empty field names, 16 MiB documents, a nesting depth of 20, `_id` types and size, Date range, and regular expression options. |
| Enterprise-only values on a Standard edition database | **Verified** (error text UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-11-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/docs/concepts/data-types>)) | `TestFirestoreEnterpriseOnlyValues`, the official Firestore Go client: Google's "Supported data types" marks 32-bit integer, BSON timestamp, bytes with subtype, Decimal128, max key, min key, ObjectId and regular expression "Supported only in Enterprise edition", and a Standard database's array cannot hold an array. The emulator, run as an Enterprise one for the MongoDB wire protocol, accepts them everywhere, so the front (`internal/firestoreadmin/edition.go`) refuses each in a Standard database's `Commit`, `BatchWrite`, `CreateDocument` and `UpdateDocument`, over gRPC and REST, a field's value or a transform's operand, `INVALID_ARGUMENT` `Value type INT is not allowed` (`OBJECT_ID`, `DECIMAL128`, `REQUEST_TIMESTAMP`, `REGEX`, `MIN_KEY`, `MAX_KEY`) and `Nested arrays are not allowed`, the Standard emulator's own errors, since Google names none; an Enterprise database stores each and reads it back. Where the Standard emulator departs from the page, the page is followed: bytes with a subtype (`BYTES_WITH_SUBTYPE`, CloudBurrow's name) and an `arrayUnion` operand are refused, and a BSON value inside a map gets its value type's error rather than the emulator's `Property v contains an invalid nested entity`. A malformed value (an `__int__` that is not an integer, a `__binary__` of subtype 0) gets the emulator's error, the same in both editions, and a query filter on such a value is answered, matching nothing, as the Standard emulator answers it. The `Write` stream, the Firebase client SDKs' channel (#1738), is passed on by the front message by message and checked request by request: the Firebase Web SDK (`firebase` 13.2.0, its Node build, over gRPC) is refused each value `invalid-argument` with the same message on `(default)`, and stores and reads back each on an Enterprise database (`test/compat-node/firestore-edition.test.mjs`, `make compat-node`); a refused request never reaches the emulator, so none of its writes apply. In a browser the SDK opens the same stream over WebChannel (#1744), plain HTTP requests on `/google.firestore.v1.Firestore/Write/channel` naming the database: on a Standard database the front passes each session on, reading its forward-channel POSTs request by request, and a request carrying such a value goes no further, with none after it, while its refusal goes down the session's backchannel as the stream's error message, `INVALID_ARGUMENT` with the same message in Google's JSON error (`{"error":{"code":400,"message":...,"status":"INVALID_ARGUMENT"}}`), which the SDK raises as the same `invalid-argument`; the Firebase Web SDK's browser build (`firebase` 13.2.0's `@firebase/firestore` `index.esm.js`, on the Fetch API, `useFetchStreams`) is refused each value on `(default)`, nothing is stored, and an Enterprise database stores and reads back each (`test/compat-node/firestore-edition-webchannel.test.mjs`, `TestEditionGuardWriteChannel`). `Listen` carries queries alone, which Standard answers, over either transport. |
| Commands Google does not list | **Verified** (refused) | `TestFirestoreMongoDB`: `collMod` is `CommandNotFound` (59), as every command Google does not list is; so are `w` other than `1` and `majority`, read concerns other than `snapshot`, `majority` and `linearizable`, and the `secondary` read preference, as Google refuses them. Error codes and messages are MongoDB's where Google documents none. |
| Sessions and multi-document transactions (`startTransaction`, `commitTransaction`, `abortTransaction`) | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDBTransactions` (#1738), through the official MongoDB Go driver: as Google documents them, optimistic concurrency with snapshot isolation. A transaction's writes are invisible until it commits and then all visible, to the driver and to the official Firestore client alike (one Firestore `Commit` with update-time preconditions); an aborted one writes nothing; its reads see its snapshot, and a write another client made since fails its commit `WriteConflict` (112) with the `TransientTransactionError` label, which `WithTransaction` retries; a command MongoDB refuses in a transaction is refused. Google's 270 s lifetime and 60 s idle expiry are enforced (unit-tested). |
| The positional update operators (`$`, `$[]`, `$[<identifier>]`) and `arrayFilters`, and the positional projection | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDBPositional` (#1738), through the official driver. |
| `$lookup` with `let` and a pipeline, and collection-less aggregations (`$documents`) | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDBLookupPipeline` (#1738), through the official driver. |
| `explain` (of `find`, `aggregate`, `count`, `distinct`, `update`, `delete`, `findAndModify`; `queryPlanner`, `executionStats`, `allPlansExecution`) | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDBExplain` (#1738), through the official driver: `find`, `aggregate`, `count` and `update` in each verbosity; the plan is a tree of the nodes Google's Query Explain page names. Console: **Query Explain (MongoDB)** on an Enterprise database's page runs it for a find or an aggregate (`TestConsoleFirestoreTextIndexAndExplain`, `TestFirestoreTextIndexAndExplainThroughThePage` in Chrome). The plan's shape is CloudBurrow's where Google's page gives no example (UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-11-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/firestore/mongodb-compatibility/docs/query-explain>)). |
| Text indexes and `$text` | **Verified** | `TestFirestoreMongoDBText` (#1738), through the official driver: a text index (an Admin API search-config index, its default language, language override and partition field), `$text` in `find` and `aggregate` with Google's search string syntax, and `{$meta: "textScore"}`. Console: **Create index** makes a text index (text fields, the MongoDB compatible API scope, a language) and the Indexes tab shows it (`TestConsoleFirestoreTextIndexAndExplain`, `TestFirestoreTextIndexAndExplainThroughThePage`). The score is CloudBurrow's own (a term-frequency score); Google does not document its formula. |

### BigQuery is a community emulator

`--services bigquery` runs [`goccy/bigquery-emulator`](https://github.com/goccy/bigquery-emulator)
0.8.1 (MIT), **built by CloudBurrow from its source with patches to the SQL engine it links**
(#1061): the CLI embeds linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 builds made from Go modules pinned and
checked by checksum, and `up` builds its image locally; nothing is pulled but the digest-pinned
base. The patches fix table functions (#1043, #1047), `DROP TABLE FUNCTION` (#976), a RECORD
inside a REPEATED RECORD (#900, upstream's open goccy/googlesqlite#76), a FLOAT64 NaN (#1066)
and an infinity inside an ARRAY or STRUCT (#1077), BYTES that are not UTF-8 text (#1075), the
`-` operator on a column, the engine's memory past 2 GiB (#989), its growth through DDL
(#1057, upstream's open goccy/googlesqlite#80), functions of another dataset (#1107, #1123) and by
one quoted path (#1122), INTERVAL signs and comparison (#1126, #1120), NULL arguments (#1109,
#1121), GEOGRAPHY text (#1119) and REPEATED fields a row leaves out (#1124); [third_party/bigquery-emulator/PROVENANCE.md](../third_party/bigquery-emulator/PROVENANCE.md)
lists each. Where a row below says "the pinned emulator" or "measured first", it was measured
against the unpatched v0.8.1. **Google publishes no BigQuery
emulator**, so this is the one opt-in backend that is neither Google's nor the real engine. It runs
ZetaSQL, so it accepts GoogleSQL, but the only fidelity claimed is what is listed below.

The coverage page lists every method of the official generated client (`google.golang.org/api/bigquery/v2`), 47; a method no annotated test covers is Unknown, and nothing is claimed for it (#993). |

The client got `UNAVAILABLE` "error reading from server: EOF", Kubernetes restarted the container, and every dataset, table and job was gone (the emulator keeps them in memory, row *Persistence*). A `DATETIME` column failed too ("invalid timestamp string"), and the session's Arrow type for a `DATETIME` was a timestamp in UTC, which the Go client read as a `time.Time`. **Now the emulator's `ReadRows` is never called:** `CreateReadSession` goes to the emulator, which reads the table and its schema by the whole name, and the front writes every stream's rows itself, from a `jobs.query` of `` SELECT <the session's columns> FROM `dataset.table` WHERE (<row_restriction>) `` (the front's own query, left out of `jobs.list`), in the session's schema: Arrow as BigQuery frames it (next row but two), a `REPEATED` column a list and a RECORD a struct at any depth, a `DATETIME` a timestamp with no zone, which is how the Go client tells one from a `TIMESTAMP` (its `arrow.go`); at most 1000 rows an answer, the schema in the first ([ReadRowsResponse](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/storage/rpc/google.cloud.bigquery.storage.v1#readrowsresponse)); `offset` skips rows. `CreateReadSession` without a `read_session` (whose field the emulator's handler reads without looking, a panic too), a table name or a format of `ARROW` or `AVRO` is **`INVALID_ARGUMENT`** before the emulator sees it. Rows are read when `ReadRows` asks, not as a snapshot at the session's creation; each `ReadRows` is one query, whose result the emulator keeps with its job (in memory) until it restarts. Units `TestStorageReadRowsAreWrittenByTheFront`, `TestStorageReadRowsInBatches`, `TestStorageReadRefusesWhatWouldCrashTheEmulator`, `TestArrowIsFramedAsBigQueryFramesIt`. |

In BigQuery a read session names its table by project, dataset and table ([ReadSession](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/storage/rpc/google.cloud.bigquery.storage.v1#readsession)). Measured first against the pinned emulator, with `one.t (s STRING)` of three rows made first and `two.t (a INT64)` of two after: `ReadRows` of a session of `two.t` failed `Unknown` "strconv.ParseInt: parsing \"one\": invalid syntax", reading `one.t`'s rows into `two.t`'s Arrow schema; the emulator reads a session's rows with `` SELECT … FROM `<tableId>` `` (its `storage_handler.go`), the bare ID, which its engine resolves to the first table of that ID in any dataset (row *Tables of one ID in two datasets*); #1032 made such a session 501. Now the front serves the Storage Read port (9060) in the emulator's pod and writes the rows itself from a query of the table's whole name (row *Storage Read API, Arrow*, #1095), so nothing of the other dataset's table is read; the emulator reads the session's schema by the whole name. In the test: `two.same (a INT64 REQUIRED, b STRING)` streamed its own two rows and `one.same (s STRING)`, made first, its three, each in its own Arrow schema; a session made before another dataset made a table of its ID read its own row; after a column was added the new column streamed; `Table.Read` and a `Query.Read` into a destination whose ID another dataset has were read through the Storage Read API (`IsAccelerated`) with their own rows. (#1046 read such a table through a view of the front's, `_cloudburrow_storage_read`; since #1095 no view is made.) The emulator names the schema's record by the namespace `<project>.<dataset>` and the table (`TableToAVRO`, `types/avro.go`), and an Avro name may hold only letters, digits and `_` ([names](https://avro.apache.org/docs/1.11.1/specification/#names)); a RECORD's record is named after its column, so two RECORD columns of one name at different depths were two records of one name, which Avro refuses too. Now the session's schema is the emulator's with every name made valid (a character a name may not have becomes `_`, a leading digit gets a `_` before it, a record whose name another has gets `_2`, `_3`…; field names, types and order unchanged), and the front writes the rows in it, in Avro's binary encoding, as it does Arrow's (row *Storage Read API, Arrow*). The console's Read-write editor runs a DML statement of its own and answers with these counts (#1024), and since #1567 an `UPDATE … FROM` and DML inside a script too, a script answered with each DML child job's counts (`TestConsoleBigQueryReadWriteEditorRunsDML`, the Console rows). |
| `bigquery.tables.patch` (`Table.Update`) from the console's Edit table: description and labels | **Verified** | `TestConsoleBigQueryEditTableViewsAndInsertOptions` (#994, #1025), through the console's Edit table, which sends `Table.Update` with only what changed (a label set or changed, a label removed as `DeleteLabel`, the description changed or emptied), read back with the official Go client, on a table and on a view: a changed label keeps the others, a removed label is gone, an emptied description reads back empty, and every label can be removed. Measured first against the pinned emulator (#1009): a patch's labels replaced the table's, a removed label was kept with an empty value and an empty description left the old one, so the form refused both; the front now patches as BigQuery does (the `tables.patch` row, `TestBigQueryTablePatchLabelsAndDescription`). |
| Scripting (`DECLARE`, multi-statement) | **Partial**: script variables are scoped to their script; other statements are claimed only where a row below says so | `TestBigQueryScriptVariablesEndWithTheScript` (#933), official Go client, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`. Measured against the pinned emulator: its SQL engine (goccy/googlesqlite v0.3.1, read from the image's binary) keeps a script's variables after the script and puts each one's value in place of every bare word naming it in **every later query of the instance**: after `DECLARE zz INT64 DEFAULT 5; SELECT zz`, a separate `SELECT zz AS v` returned 5, and after `DECLARE w INT64 DEFAULT 9`, `SELECT 1 AS w` failed with a syntax error. BigQuery scopes a variable to its script. The front sends each variable a script declares under a name of its own for that request (`renameVariables`), renaming exactly the words the engine would replace, so the script reads its variables as before (`DECLARE`, `DEFAULT` from an earlier variable, `SET`: 10 and 9 read back) and a later query gets "Unrecognized name: zz", and an alias `w` is an alias. An error naming a variable names it as the client wrote it, and `jobs.get` shows the client's text. Within the script that declares it, only the references to a variable are renamed (#956, next row). Unit `TestRenameVariables`, `TestScriptVariablesDoNotOutliveTheScript`. |
| A script variable of the name of an alias, a column or a table in its script | **Verified** for an alias, a column list, a STRUCT field and a subquery column of another name; **Not implemented** (501) where BigQuery may read the other name | `TestBigQueryScriptVariableNamedAsAnAlias` (#956), official Go client, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`. Measured against the pinned emulator: within its own script, its engine (goccy/googlesqlite v0.3.1, `substituteScriptVariables`) put a variable's value in place of every bare word of its name before reading a statement, so `DECLARE n INT64 DEFAULT 1; SELECT 2 AS n` failed "Syntax error: Unexpected integer literal "1"", where BigQuery returns 2. The front renames only the words that refer to the variable (`renameVariables`, with its lexer): an alias after `AS` or in place of one, a table's, CTE's or function's name, a column in a `CREATE TABLE`'s or `INSERT`'s column list, a `STRUCT<…>` field, a column in `EXCEPT (…)` or `USING (…)`, and a column `UPDATE … SET` assigns keep the client's name, which the engine does not touch. Read back: `SELECT 2 AS n` returned 2; `SELECT n + 1 AS m, 3 n2` 2 and 3; `SELECT n, m FROM (SELECT 7 AS m) AS t` 1 and 7; `DECLARE s STRUCT<n INT64> …; SELECT s.n AS n` 5; `INSERT INTO t (a, n) VALUES (n, 4)` wrote 3 and 4. BigQuery's documentation does not say which of a variable and a column, alias or range variable of one name a query reads ([procedural language](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/procedural-language) says only that variable names are case-insensitive), so a statement that refers to a variable is **501 `notImplemented`**, before anything of the script runs, when the name is also one there: an alias or range variable it defines, a column after a `.`, a column of a table it reads (looked up with `tables.get`, or, for a table an earlier statement of the script makes, from its column list or its select list), or a table it reads whose columns are not known (measured cases: `SELECT n FROM (SELECT 7 AS n)`, `SELECT a FROM t WHERE a = n` with a column `n` in `t`, `INSERT INTO t (a) SELECT n FROM t`). Unit `TestRenameVariables`, `TestSelectColumns`. |
| A script that fails after a statement that changes data | **Verified** as a query job (`jobs.insert`) without a transaction, and (#1459) through `jobs.query`, for a script with a `TEMP` table or function too (`TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`); **Not implemented** (501) as a query job with `BEGIN TRANSACTION` or `COMMIT` in a transaction the front does not carry out (since #1201 the front carries out every other transaction, row `Multi-statement transactions`) | `TestBigQueryFailedScriptKeepsItsTable` (#935, #955), `TestBigQueryEveryScriptInTurn`, `TestBigQueryFailedScriptLeavesTheCatalogInStep` (#1459), official Go client, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`. BigQuery keeps what a script's statements did before the one that fails. Measured against the pinned emulator: **through `jobs.query`** it runs a script in one transaction and rolls all of it back (`CREATE TABLE ds.e1 AS SELECT 1 AS a; SELECT * FROM nope.nope; CREATE TABLE ds.e2 …` failed 400 and `ds.e1` did not exist; the same for `INSERT`, and for a runtime error, `ERROR('boom')`); **as a query job** it commits what the statements before the failing one did, as it records the failed job in the script's transaction (after `INSERT INTO ds.t VALUES (9); SELECT * FROM nope.nope`, `ds.t` had the row; through `jobs.query`, it did not), and the job fails with the statement's error. So through `jobs.query`, when a script with a statement that changes data (anything but a query, `DECLARE`, `SET`, `ASSERT`, a `TEMP` table and DML on one) and a statement after it fails, the answer is **501 `notImplemented`** naming the emulator's error; as a query job, the job fails with the emulator's error, as in BigQuery, and `ds.e1` exists (read back), unless the script has a transaction, which BigQuery rolls back and the emulator does not undo: then the job is `DONE` with a 501 `notImplemented` `errorResult`. Either way the emulator's catalog and its list of tables are then put back in step with its tables (#955, row below). Since #1249, a script whose failing statement is a query before its last (as `CREATE TABLE ds.e1 …; SELECT * FROM nope.nope; CREATE TABLE ds.e2 …`) is run statement by statement instead (row below): through `jobs.query` too it fails with the statement's error and `ds.e1` is kept, as in BigQuery (read back). Since #1459 every script of several statements with no `TEMP` table or function is carried out by the front a statement at a time (row `Statements beside a TEMP table`), so through `jobs.query` too it fails with the failing statement's error and keeps what the statements before it did, as BigQuery does (read back: after `INSERT INTO t VALUES (5); INSERT INTO nope …; INSERT INTO t VALUES (6)`, `t` held `[5]`; a dropped table stayed dropped and a made one stayed made); so is a script with a `TEMP` table or function, run as its session's text (`TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`). A failed script that changes nothing kept, and a syntax error (which fails a script before anything runs, in BigQuery too), are answered with the emulator's error as before. Units `TestFailedScriptKeepsWhatItWrote`, `TestScriptsCarriedOutInTurn`. |
| A runtime error in a query that is not a script's last statement | **Verified** (#1249) through `jobs.query` and as a query job, for a script with no control flow, and (#1459) with a `TEMP` table or function, its `TEMP` tables then the hidden tables of the script's session (row `Statements beside a TEMP table`) | `TestBigQueryScriptRuntimeErrorBeforeLast` (#1249), `TestBigQueryStatementsInTempScripts` (#1459), official Go client. Measured first against the pinned emulator, through the front: `INSERT INTO ds.t VALUES (5); SELECT 1/0; INSERT INTO ds.t VALUES (6)` answered done and kept both rows; the emulator reads only the rows of a script's last statement, so an earlier query's runtime error is never raised. BigQuery fails the script at that statement and keeps what the statements before it did. So a script whose statements before its last include a query (`SELECT`, `WITH`, a parenthesized query) is carried out by the front as a script with control flow is (`internal/bigqueryfront/scriptflow.go`, `earlierQuery`): each statement is a request of its own, and the script fails at the first that fails, with that statement's error (read back: the row of the `INSERT` before it kept, the one after it not run). Its answer is the last query's rows, as before, also when a `DECLARE`, `SET` or `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE … INTO` follows it (#1037). A `TEMP` table or function lasts only for the request that made it, so such a script was 501 until #1459 ran it as its session's text. (`ASSERT`: row below, #1253.) Since #1201 a transaction the front carries out has each statement probed, so its queries' errors are seen (row `Multi-statement transactions`). Unit `TestFailedScriptKeepsWhatItWrote`, `TestEarlierQuery`. |
| `ASSERT expression [AS description]` | **Verified** (#1253) alone and in a script, through `jobs.query` and as a query job, and (#1459) in a script with a `TEMP` table or function | `TestBigQueryAssert` (#1253), `TestBigQueryStatementsInTempScripts` (#1459), official Go client. Measured first against the pinned emulator, through the front: `ASSERT FALSE` answered done with no rows and `ASSERT FALSE; SELECT 1` the row `1`; the emulator does not check an `ASSERT` at all. BigQuery fails the query when the expression is `FALSE` or `NULL`, with the description in the error message ([debugging statements](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/debugging-statements#assert)). So a script with an `ASSERT`, or a lone one, is carried out by the front, as a script with a query before its last is (row above; `scriptflow.go`, `assert`): it runs `SELECT (expression)` as a query of its own; `TRUE` goes on, `FALSE` or `NULL` fails the query 400 `invalidQuery` with `Assertion failed: ` and the description, or the expression's text without one (the reference says only that the description appears in the message, and its examples show the description alone after `Error:`; the `Assertion failed: ` prefix is not quoted there, so a test reading the message should match the description). Read back: a runtime error in the expression fails it with that error, the `INSERT` before a failed `ASSERT` is kept and the one after it never runs, an `ASSERT` inside `IF` is checked, a `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` handler catches it with that `@@error.message`, and `ASSERT TRUE; SELECT 2` answers `2`. An expression that is not a `BOOL`, or a description that is not a `STRING` literal, is refused 400. A `TEMP` table or function lasts only for one request, so such a script was 501 until #1459 (row `Statements beside a TEMP table`). Unit `TestScriptAssert`. |
| The tables after a failed script | **Verified** for the tables and views a script's `CREATE` and `DROP` statements name, and its `TEMP` tables; functions and `DROP SCHEMA` are the next row | `TestBigQueryFailedScriptLeavesTheCatalogInStep` (#955), official Go client, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`. Measured against the pinned emulator, a failed script left, for every later query, its SQL engine's catalog (goccy/googlesqlite v0.3.1) or its list of tables (`tables.get`, `tables.list`) out of step with its tables. The engine changes its in-memory catalog as each statement runs and reloads it only from catalog rows updated since it last did (`Catalog.Sync`: `WHERE updatedAt >= lastSyncedAt`), so a rollback puts the rows back and not the catalog; the emulator updates its list of tables from a query only when the query succeeded. Through `jobs.query` (rolled back): after `DROP TABLE ds.keep; SELECT * FROM nope.nope`, `ds.keep` was listed and `SELECT a FROM ds.keep` failed "Table not found"; after `CREATE TABLE ds.c1 AS SELECT 1 AS a; …`, `SELECT * FROM ds.c1` failed "sqlite3: SQL logic error: no such table"; after `DROP TABLE ds.keep2; CREATE TABLE ds.keep2 (z STRING); …`, `SELECT a FROM ds.keep2` failed "Unrecognized name: a"; after `CREATE TEMP TABLE ghost AS SELECT 1 AS a; …`, the next `CREATE TEMP TABLE ghost AS SELECT 2 AS b; SELECT b FROM ghost` failed "Unrecognized name: b". As a query job (committed): a dropped table was still listed and not found by a query, and a table made was read by a query and not listed. After a failure the front puts them back with statements of its own (`resyncCatalog`; each measured): rolled back, the catalog is made to match the list (a listed table is taken out of the catalog by a script that drops it and fails, which `jobs.query` rolls back, and added again by `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` from its schema, which leaves the table and its rows; one not listed is dropped `IF EXISTS`); committed, the list is made to match the catalog (a table the engine reads and the list lacks is added again from the engine's columns, which lists it; a listed one the engine lacks is created and dropped, which unlists it; one listed with other columns is patched). Read back through `jobs.query`: `ds.keep` with a STRUCT and an ARRAY, `ds.keep2` and a view as before the scripts, `ds.c1` "not found" and then made again, and a new `ghost` with its own columns; as a query job: `ds.keep` and the view gone, `ds.keep2` listed and read with the new column `z`, `ds.c1` listed and read. The engine's copy of a table put back is made from its schema (names, types, modes, defaults), without its options; the front's statements are recorded by the emulator as jobs, as its other checks are. No upstream issue found (goccy/bigquery-emulator, goccy/googlesqlite, as of 2026-09-28). Unit `TestFailedScriptResyncsTheCatalog`. |
| Functions after a failed script, and `DROP SCHEMA` | **Verified** for `CREATE [OR REPLACE] [TABLE] FUNCTION` and (#1459) `DROP [TABLE] FUNCTION` in a script given to `jobs.query`, one with a `TEMP` table or function too (`TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`), and for a failed query job; `DROP SCHEMA` is carried out (#990, row below) | `TestBigQueryFailedScriptFunctionsAndDropSchema` (#976, #1459), official Go client, through `jobs.query` (`Query.Read`) and `jobs.insert`. Measured first against the pinned emulator: its engine adds a function to its in-memory catalog as `CREATE FUNCTION` runs and takes it out as `DROP FUNCTION` runs, and a rollback does not put that back. Through `jobs.query`, after `CREATE FUNCTION ds.f(x INT64) AS (x + 1); SELECT * FROM nope.nope` (answered 501, "nothing the script did was kept") `SELECT ds.f(1)` read 2, and so for `CREATE TABLE FUNCTION`; after `DROP FUNCTION ds.g; …`, `ds.g(1)` failed "Function not found". As a query job both were kept, as BigQuery keeps what the statements before the failing one did. So, for a script of several statements given to `jobs.query`: each function a `CREATE [OR REPLACE] FUNCTION` makes is looked up before the script runs (calling it with no arguments: "Function not found" or "No matching signature", measured), and when the script fails, each that did not exist is taken out of the catalog again by a script that drops it and fails, which `jobs.query` rolls back: `f(1)` is then "not found", and the same `CREATE FUNCTION` run later makes it with its new body (`f(1)` read 3). A function that existed before is left as it was (`g(1)` still 10). A table function is taken out the same way, with `DROP TABLE FUNCTION`, which the engine CloudBurrow builds carries out (#1061): after `CREATE TABLE FUNCTION ds.tf …; SELECT * FROM nope.nope` (501), `ds.tf(1)` is "not found", and made again it reads its new body; the pinned emulator refused `DROP TABLE FUNCTION` (400 "Statement not supported: DropTableFunctionStatement", and `DROP FUNCTION` of one left it callable, measured), so this was 501 before anything ran. A `DROP [TABLE] FUNCTION` in such a script was 501 too (the emulator has no `routines.get`, so the function cannot be read to be made again), and since #1459 the script is run as its session's text, a statement at a time (`TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`). A query job is sent as it is (`k(1)` read 6 after its failed job). `DROP SCHEMA` the emulator refuses alone and in a script, through both (measured: 400 "currently unsupported DROP SCHEMA statement", and the dataset and its tables were kept), so a failed script never ran one; since #990 the front carries it out through `datasets.delete` after the query succeeds, and keeps the dataset when the script fails (row `DROP SCHEMA` below; this test's 501 for it is gone). `CREATE FUNCTION` of a function that exists, and `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` of one, are the row after it (#986). Since #1459 a script with no `TEMP` table or function is carried out a statement at a time instead, each statement as it runs alone, and (#1459) so is a script with one, run as its session's text (`TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`); through `jobs.query` a failed script with none keeps the function it made (`f(1)` read 2), the one it replaced (`g(1)` read 2) and the table function (`tf(1)` read 1), and a `DROP FUNCTION` before a failing statement is kept (`g(1)` then "not found"), as BigQuery keeps what the statements before the failing one did (read back). Units `TestFailedScriptFunctions`, `TestDropSchema`, `TestScriptsCarriedOutInTurn`. |
| `DROP SCHEMA` | **Verified** alone and in a script whose other statements do not name the dataset, `CASCADE` and `RESTRICT`, `IF EXISTS`, and (#1459) in any script of several statements, with a `TEMP` table or function or not, carried out in its turn (`TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`) | `TestBigQueryDropSchema` (#990), `TestBigQueryDropSchemaCascadeDropsTableFunctions` (#1061) and `TestBigQueryEveryScriptInTurn` (#1459: `CREATE SCHEMA s; CREATE TABLE s.t …; DROP SCHEMA s CASCADE` left no `s`), official Go client, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`. BigQuery deletes the dataset, with `CASCADE` its tables, views and functions, and with `RESTRICT` (the default) "only if it's empty. Otherwise, returns an error" ([DDL](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-definition-language#drop_schema_statement)). Measured first against the pinned emulator: every `DROP SCHEMA`, `IF EXISTS` of a dataset that does not exist too, was 400 "currently unsupported DROP SCHEMA statement" (501 in the front since #976). Its `datasets.delete` does delete a dataset: without `deleteContents` it refuses one with a table, 400 `resourceInUse` "Dataset project:ds is still in use", and with it the tables go too; it does not count a dataset's functions, and leaves them callable after the dataset is gone (`ds.f(1)` still read 2) until a `DROP FUNCTION`; its engine has no `routines.list` (500 "unsupported") nor `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES`. So the front sends the statement as one that does nothing and, when the query succeeds, deletes the dataset through `datasets.delete` (with `deleteContents` for `CASCADE`) and drops each function it knows in the dataset: one it saw a `CREATE FUNCTION` statement or `routines.insert` make, and, since #1001, one a `CREATE FUNCTION` of the emulator's jobs from before the front started made (the emulator keeps every job and its query in memory while it runs, so a front whose container restarted reads them there: `jobs.list`, then `jobs.get` of each job older than the front, once per project). **Since #1115 a restart of the front's container does not scan again**: what the front knows of the functions, and that it has scanned, is kept in a file on the pod's emptyDir beside the Storage Write streams (unit `TestKnownFunctionsOutliveAFrontRestart`). Measured before: on an instance with 587 jobs, the first `DROP SCHEMA` after a restart of the front's container took 97 seconds, past the Go client's deadline in `TestBigQueryDropSchemaCascadeDropsTableFunctions`. A front that starts without the file (a new pod, whose emulator has no jobs, or an unreadable file) still scans (#1135). Measured for #1001: the engine has no other list of its functions (`routines.get` is 404 even for a function `routines.insert` made, and a GoogleSQL query cannot read the engine's catalog table, "Table not found"), and `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` makes none, since the emulator runs no `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` at all (#1011). **Not found**, and so left callable after `CASCADE` and not counted for `RESTRICT`: a function made through `routines.insert` before the front's container last restarted. Read back: an empty dataset is dropped by `DROP SCHEMA`; one with a table and a function by `DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS … CASCADE`, after which the function is "not found" and the dataset made again has no table `t`; `DROP SCHEMA` of one with a table fails `resourceInUse` (400 through `jobs.query`, a failed query job) and the table keeps its row; of one that does not exist, `notFound` (404), or with `IF EXISTS` nothing; `SELECT 1; DROP SCHEMA d CASCADE; SELECT 2` drops it. A dataset whose only content is a function the front saw made fails `DROP SCHEMA` (`RESTRICT`) `resourceInUse` too, and so does one whose only content is a function `Routine.Create` (`routines.insert`) made, which `CASCADE` then drops with it (`TestBigQueryDropSchemaDropsRoutinesInsertFunctions`, #1001; the function called before, "Function not found" after). When the script fails the drop is kept since #1459, as BigQuery keeps what the statements before the failure did: `DROP SCHEMA d CASCADE; SELECT * FROM nope.nope` fails and `d` is gone, through `jobs.query` and as a query job (it was 501, as the emulator rolled the whole script back, #935); a later statement naming the dropped dataset fails "not found", and `SELECT 1; DROP SCHEMA d CASCADE; SELECT 2` drops it (`TestBigQueryDropSchema`, `TestBigQueryEveryScriptInTurn`). **501**, nothing run, where the script is not carried out a statement at a time (`internal/bigqueryfront/dropschema.go`): a script whose other statements name the dataset (or whose default dataset it is), a `DROP SCHEMA` in an `EXCEPTION` handler or after a `RETURN`, one that would fail (not found, not empty) after other statements, and anything after the dataset's name other than `CASCADE` or `RESTRICT`. A table function the front knows in the dataset is dropped with `DROP TABLE FUNCTION` since #1061 (501 before: the pinned engine refused it): `RESTRICT` of a dataset holding one fails `resourceInUse`, `CASCADE` drops it, a call is then "not found", and the dataset made again has none (`TestBigQueryDropSchemaCascadeDropsTableFunctions`). Unit `TestDropSchema`, and `TestDropSchemaFindsEveryFunction` (#1001: a function `routines.insert` made, and ones in jobs from before the front started, one named through the job's default dataset; a job after its start is not read). |
| Copy jobs (`Table.CopierFrom`) | **Verified** within a project, and between projects (#1764: a table of another project than the job's, as source or destination, `TestBigQueryServesEveryResourceManagerProject`), one or several sources, every `writeDisposition` and `createDisposition`; `operationType` `CLONE` into a new table, and `SNAPSHOT` and `RESTORE` (#1002, below; the same through DDL, `CREATE TABLE … CLONE` row); Copy table on the console offers each `operationType` (#1002) and an optional destination project (#1767); **Not implemented** (501) where noted | `TestBigQueryCopyJobs` (#987), official Go client. Measured first: the emulator answered a copy job **400** "unspecified job configuration query", `jobInternalError`, and copied nothing (it runs only query, load and extract jobs). The front now carries it out as a job of its own (answered by the front, as the extracts it writes are), with `statistics.copy.copiedRows`: a new destination is made through `tables.insert` with the first source's schema (a DDL `CREATE TABLE` would not keep `REQUIRED`: measured, `NOT NULL` read back `NULLABLE`), made as every `tables.insert` is since #1000, a `FLOAT` column as `FLOAT64` (next row); the rows are written by one `INSERT … SELECT … UNION ALL SELECT …` of the sources. Read back: two sources with a `REQUIRED` column, a `RECORD` with a `REPEATED` field, `FLOAT64`, `TIMESTAMP` with microseconds and `NUMERIC` copied into a new table hold the same rows (`TO_JSON_STRING` of each) and its schema reads back as the sources' (names, types, modes, a description), and takes a `FLOAT64` insert; `jobs.get` and `jobs.list` read the job back. `WRITE_EMPTY` (the default) into a table with rows fails `duplicate` and leaves it; `WRITE_APPEND` adds; `WRITE_TRUNCATE` replaces rows and schema (written to a scratch table first, so a failure keeps the destination; the destination is then deleted and made again from the source's schema); `CREATE_NEVER` of a missing table and a missing source fail `notFound`, and nothing is made; a view as a source fails `invalid`. `operationType` `CLONE` of one table into one that does not exist (#1002): the rows are copied and the destination made with a `cloneDefinition` (the source, and the job's start as `cloneTime`), which the emulator keeps (measured) and `tables.get` reads back; the clone is a writable `TABLE`, and an `INSERT` into it leaves its base as it was (`TestBigQueryCopyJobs`); a later schema change that remakes the table (#1036) does not keep it. **501**, nothing copied: a `SNAPSHOT`, `RESTORE` or `CLONE` of several tables, a `CLONE` into a table that exists (not given by the documentation), `destinationEncryptionConfiguration` of or into a partition (decorator) (#1762: a whole table's key is the next row but one), `destinationExpirationTime` into a table that exists (whether it changes that table's expiration is not documented), a `WRITE_APPEND` (or `WRITE_EMPTY` into an empty table) whose destination's schema differs from the source's (BigQuery's rules for which differences it accepts are not in its documentation), a view as the destination, and a dry run (#1002). **`destinationExpirationTime`** (#1002, an RFC 3339 time or milliseconds) is given to a new destination as its `expirationTime`, which `tables.get` reads back: `bq cp --snapshot --expiration=3600` makes a snapshot that expires in an hour (`TestBqCopySnapshotCloneAndRestore`, the real `bq` CLI through the harness, read back by the official Go client, which also reads back `bq cp --clone` and `bq cp --restore`); as for any table's `expirationTime`, the emulator does not delete the table when it passes; a value that is not a time fails `invalid`. Several sources whose schemas are not identical fail the job, `invalid` (BigQuery's documentation: all source tables must have identical schemas; its message is UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/managing-tables>)), and nothing is copied (#1002). **Why the destination is deleted even when its schema is the source's (#1092, closed):** the front could empty it with `DELETE … WHERE true` and insert the rows, which spares the engine's catalog rebuild of a `DROP TABLE` (*The SQL engine failing* row), only if that gave what BigQuery gives, and BigQuery's documentation does not say what a copy with `WRITE_TRUNCATE` does to the destination's description, labels, expiration or creation time: the copy configuration says only "If the table already exists, BigQuery overwrites the table data and uses the schema and table constraints from the source table" ([JobConfigurationTableCopy.writeDisposition](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/Job#JobConfigurationTableCopy)), and Copy tables says "If the copy operation overwrites an existing table, then the table-level access for the existing table is maintained. Tags from the source table aren't copied to the overwritten table, while tags on the existing table are retained" ([managing-tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/managing-tables#copy-table)), which the emulator has neither of; row access policies are overwritten and policy tags removed ([row-level-security-intro](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/row-level-security-intro), [column-level-security-intro](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/column-level-security-intro)), which the emulator has neither of either. Whether the destination keeps its own description, labels and expiration or takes none cannot be read, and CloudBurrow does not measure against BigQuery, so the front does not change what it does on a guess. Unit `TestCopyJobs`. |
| Copy jobs: the destination's partitioning and clustering (`bigquery.jobs.insert`, `bigquery.jobs.get`, `bigquery.tables.get`) | **Verified** (#1759), as managing-partitioned-tables documents it ("Copy a partitioned table", read 2026-11-17). A new destination is partitioned and clustered as the source ("All of the partitioning information is copied with the table", "all of the clustering information"): time-unit column, integer-range and ingestion-time partitioning, with the partition expiration and `requirePartitionFilter`, and the schema's descriptions. Several sources must share their partitioning and clustering, and a mix of partitioned and non-partitioned sources fails the job. Into a table that exists: different partitioning or clustering fails the job. A non-partitioned source into a column- or range-partitioned table also fails ("only supported for ingestion-time partitioning"). A non-partitioned source into an ingestion-time partitioned table lands in today's partition. A partitioned source into a non-partitioned table leaves it unpartitioned ("remains unpartitioned"), `WRITE_TRUNCATE` included. Since #1137 `@@dataset_id` in a query with a default dataset reads that dataset's ID (the emulator read NULL; the front sends it as a string literal unless the query `SET`s it), unit `TestDatasetIDVariable`, compat `TestBigQueryDatasetIDIsTheDefaultDataset`. |
