| Materialized views: `CREATE [OR REPLACE] MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF NOT EXISTS] … [PARTITION BY] [CLUSTER BY] [OPTIONS(…)] AS`, `ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF EXISTS] … SET OPTIONS`, `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF EXISTS]`, `CALL BQ.REFRESH_MATERIALIZED_VIEW`, `tables.insert` with a `materializedView` (#1390) | **Verified** for each, as a lone statement, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`, and (#1415) in a multi-statement script, each a child job, with a TEMP table or function too (#1434); a query of one reads current data after a change to a base table, its `max_staleness` honoured, and the automatic refresh sets `lastRefreshTime` (#1415); **Not implemented** (501): the statements in a dry run of a script with a TEMP table or function; not built: smart tuning's rewrite of a query of a base table to read the view (an optimization, same results; whether BigQuery chooses a view is its cost estimate, `rejectedReason` `COST`, which Google does not document, #1456) | `TestBigQueryMaterializedViews` (#1390), official Go client. Measured first: `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` and `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` failed 400 "Statement not supported" (the front refused them 501), and `tables.insert` with a `materializedView` made an ordinary view, its query run at every read. The front makes a materialized view as a backing table in the hidden results dataset, made by `CREATE TABLE … AS` its query, and the engine's view of it, whose resource it gives the type `MATERIALIZED_VIEW` and a `materializedView` definition (`query`, `enableRefresh`, `refreshIntervalMs`, `lastRefreshTime`, `allowNonIncrementalDefinition`; `max_staleness` as the table's `maxStaleness`). Read back with `Table.Metadata`: `Type` `MATERIALIZED_VIEW`, the query as written, `EnableRefresh`, `RefreshInterval` (`refresh_interval_minutes = 60`: one hour), `LastRefreshTime`, the `description`. **Refresh and staleness** (#1415): BigQuery answers a query of a materialized view with current data, combining its cached results with the base tables' changes, unless `max_staleness` lets it return the last refresh's ([materialized views](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-intro#materialized_views_and_staleness)). At each query of one, and each `tables.get`, the front compares the backing table with its query's results now (their row count and two sums of the rows' fingerprints): when a base table changed since the last refresh, and `enable_refresh` and its refresh interval (30 minutes by default) has passed by the front's clock (the admin's `clock:advance` moves it), it refreshes it and sets `lastRefreshTime`; otherwise a query reads current data, the backing table brought up to date without a refresh (`lastRefreshTime` kept), unless the last refresh is within `max_staleness`, when it reads the last refresh's. The test: a row inserted into the base table is in the next read, `lastRefreshTime` unchanged; `CALL BQ.REFRESH_MATERIALIZED_VIEW('ds.mv')` moves it; after another insert and 61 minutes, `Table.Metadata` shows a later `lastRefreshTime`; with `enable_refresh = FALSE, max_staleness = INTERVAL 2 HOUR`, a read 61 minutes after the last refresh gives its results, one 121 minutes after gives current ones, and `lastRefreshTime` does not move. BigQuery refreshes within about five minutes of a change; the front refreshes at the first query or `tables.get` once due, so `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.MATERIALIZED_VIEWS` shows the refresh after one of those. **In a script** (#1415, the same test): `CREATE TABLE`, `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW … OPTIONS (enable_refresh = FALSE)`, `ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW … SET OPTIONS (description = …)`, `ALTER TABLE … SET OPTIONS`, `INSERT`, `CALL BQ.REFRESH_MATERIALIZED_VIEW` and a `SELECT` of the view in one script: the front runs it a statement at a time, each statement as a lone one, with child jobs of `statementType` `CREATE_MATERIALIZED_VIEW`, `ALTER_MATERIALIZED_VIEW` and `CALL` (#1353); the script's rows are the view's current sum, and the options read back; `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` in a script deletes it. **With a TEMP table or function** (#1434, `TestBigQueryMaterializedViewsInTempScripts`, official Go client, `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`; **measured first**: each such script was 501): BigQuery keeps a TEMP table for the script ([temporary tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/multi-statement-queries#temporary_tables)), but here one lasts only for the engine request that made it, and the materialized view statements are a request each. So, as `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` DDL in such a script is served as the text it amounts to (#1416), the script is run as the text it amounts to: each TEMP table is a table of the hidden dataset for the script (each name of it where a table is named is its path, `AS` its own name), each TEMP function a function there, and that text is run a statement at a time as above, with child jobs; the tables and functions are deleted when the script ends, failed or not. The test: a script that makes a TEMP table and a TEMP function, fills a base table from them, makes a materialized view of it, writes the TEMP table again, alters and refreshes the view, and selects from both answers the view's sum and the TEMP table's rows; the view's options read back; the child jobs have `statementType` `CREATE_MATERIALIZED_VIEW`, `ALTER_MATERIALIZED_VIEW`, `CALL` and `INSERT`, and their texts name the TEMP table as the script does; a later query of the TEMP table fails; the reverse order (`DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW`, then a TEMP table read after it) works too. A materialized view whose query reads the TEMP table is **400**, nothing run (BigQuery's views read base tables; wording CloudBurrow's, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-create>)). Known limits: a TEMP table named as a column where a table is named is not rewritten; a dry run of such a script stays **501**. Since #1459 a TEMP table named inside an `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` string is the script's. Units `TestMVScriptsAndStaleness`, `TestTempSessionScript`. `ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW SET OPTIONS` sets `enable_refresh`, `refresh_interval_minutes`, `max_staleness`, `allow_non_incremental_definition` and the table options. `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.MATERIALIZED_VIEWS` lists it with its `last_refresh_time` and `refresh_watermark`; `TABLE_OPTIONS` gives its options and `TABLES` its `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` DDL. `tables.insert` with a `MaterializedViewDefinition` makes one as `CREATE` does (`RefreshInterval` two hours read back). `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` deletes it and its backing table (as `tables.delete` does); of none it is **404 `notFound`**, nothing with `IF EXISTS`; of a table that is not one **400**. **400 `invalidQuery`**, nothing made, for the documented limits of its query ([query limitations](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-create#query_limitations)): a non-deterministic function (`CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()`, `RAND()`, …), and, unless `allow_non_incremental_definition = TRUE`, analytic functions, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, `ARRAY_AGG`, `STRING_AGG`, `COUNT(DISTINCT …)`, and `RIGHT` or `FULL OUTER JOIN` (wording CloudBurrow's, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-create>)); a table named without a dataset is **400 `invalid`**, as for a view. The console shows a materialized view in the dataset tree with its definition (query, automatic refresh, last refreshed) and a Refresh action, and Create table makes one. https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-intro |
| Collation `und:ci` (#1508, #1516): a STRING column's `COLLATE`, a STRING's inside a STRUCT or an ARRAY, a table's and a dataset's `DEFAULT COLLATE`, `tables.insert`'s field `collation` (a RECORD's field and a REPEATED STRING too), the `COLLATE` function, `ALTER TABLE SET DEFAULT COLLATE`, a script's `CREATE TABLE` | **Verified** | `TestBigQueryCollationUndCI`, `TestBigQueryCollationDefaults`, and since #1516 `TestBigQueryNestedCollation` and `TestBigQueryCollationInScriptsAndAlter` (official Go client, `jobs.query`, `tables.insert`, `tables.get`), on a fresh instance; engine units googlesqlite `TestCollationUndCI` (patch 0059) and `TestNestedCollationUndCI` (patch 0061), bigquery-emulator `TestCollatedColumn` (patch 0049) and `TestNestedCollatedFields` (patch 0051), front units `TestQueryCollationRefusal`, `TestTableCollationRefusal`, `TestTableDefaultCollate`, `TestCollated`, `TestNestedCollationDDL`. BigQuery: a STRING with the collation `'und:ci'` compares case-insensitively, in comparisons, `IN`, `LIKE`, joins, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `MIN`/`MAX` and `COUNT(DISTINCT)`; `COLLATE(x, '')` takes it away; "A column with empty collation doesn't inherit the table's default collation"; "und:ci and empty collation are supported, but not other collation specifications" ([collation concepts](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/collation-concepts)); a new column without one inherits the table's default, and a `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT`'s collation passes through ([DDL](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-definition-language#create_table_statement)). Measured first: `CREATE TABLE … (s STRING COLLATE 'und:ci')` failed 400 "COLLATE is not supported", and a `tables.insert` column collated `und:ci` compared case-sensitively; then (#1508's first pass) a plain `CREATE TABLE` in a dataset with `DEFAULT COLLATE 'und:ci'` made a case-sensitive table (`s = 'aBC'` matched no `'Abc'`, BigQuery 1), as the front collated its metadata only after the engine made it, and `COLLATE 'und:cs'` was taken and compared by code point. Now the engine's analyzer has collation support and the catalog's column carries its collation (go-googlesql 0003, googlesqlite 0059); `tables.insert` writes each column's `COLLATE` (bigquery-emulator 0049) and a `CREATE TABLE` column's collation reads back from `tables.get`; a lone `CREATE TABLE` (and `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT`) in a dataset with a default collation gets it as its own `DEFAULT COLLATE` before it runs, and `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` gives a new STRING column its `COLLATE` or else the table's `defaultCollation`. A collation other than `'und:ci'` or `''`, in a query, a Table or a Dataset resource, is 400 with nothing made (the wording is CloudBurrow's, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/collation-concepts>)). Since #1516 a STRING inside a STRUCT or an ARRAY carries a collation, as the reference documents ("A STRING field in a STRUCT", "A STRING element in an ARRAY"): `STRUCT<a STRING COLLATE 'und:ci'>` and `ARRAY<STRING COLLATE 'und:ci'>` in `CREATE TABLE` and `ADD COLUMN`, a RECORD's field and a REPEATED STRING in `tables.insert`, and a table's or dataset's default, which reaches each STRING inside a column that names none ("A column that contains a collation-supported type ... is a collation-supported column"); a field access (`st.a`), `UNNEST`, `IN UNNEST`, a subscript, `GROUP BY`, `COUNT(DISTINCT)` and a STRUCT's `=`, `!=`, `IN` and `CASE` compare it case-insensitively, and `tables.get` and `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMN_FIELD_PATHS` read it back. Measured first: both were 501, as the engine's analyzer failed "GOOGLESQL_RET_CHECK failure ... annotations != nullptr"; googlesqlite 0061 turns its nested column annotations on and gives the catalog's column an annotation map of its type's shape, and bigquery-emulator 0051 writes a `tables.insert` field's `COLLATE` inside the column's type and reads the engine's nested collations back. A `CREATE TABLE` inside a script of several statements gets its dataset's `DEFAULT COLLATE` (or that of a `CREATE SCHEMA` earlier in the script) before the script runs, and its table the `defaultCollation`, as a lone one does (measured first: the script's table compared case-sensitively and read back none). `ALTER TABLE SET DEFAULT COLLATE 'und:ci'` or `''` sets the table's `defaultCollation`, which only the columns added after it take, in the same statement too ("The updated collation specification only applies to columns added afterwards", [DDL](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-definition-language#alter_table_collate_statement)); it was 501. `ALTER COLUMN SET DATA TYPE` keeps the column's collation, and one that names a different `COLLATE` (on the column or a field) is 400, as "You cannot update an existing collation specification on a column" (the wording is CloudBurrow's, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/collation-concepts>)). **Not supported**: a table a query, load or copy job makes is not collated. |
| `privacy_policy` of a table or view: aggregation threshold, join restriction, differential privacy (#1426, #1455, #1482, #1502, #1517) | **Verified** for the aggregation threshold, the join restriction and (#1455) differential privacy, `SELECT WITH DIFFERENTIAL_PRIVACY` and a `differential_privacy_policy` with its epsilon and delta budget, through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`; (#1482) with `HAVING`, as a subquery, a CTE's query and a script's statement, and with `group_selection_strategy = PUBLIC_GROUPS`; (#1502) an aggregation threshold or join restriction table or view read by `SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD` in a subquery, a CTE, after a `WITH` list or in `CREATE TABLE … AS`, in a script, and in joins that are not INNER; (#1517) two clauses in one query, a read with no clause in a subquery, a CTE or through a view (400), `JOIN_ANY` met by an outer join, `JOIN_ALL` alongside one, a `NATURAL` join (400), and an expression over differentially private aggregates | `TestBigQueryPrivacyPolicyAggregationThreshold`, `TestBigQueryPrivacyPolicyJoinRestriction` (#1426), `TestBigQueryPrivacyPolicyDifferentialPrivacy`, `TestBigQueryDifferentialPrivacyPolicyBudget` (#1455), `TestBigQueryDifferentialPrivacyMore` (#1482), `TestBigQueryPrivacyPolicyReads` (#1502), `TestBigQueryPrivacyPolicyRest` (#1517), official Go client (and the generated client for `tables.patch`). Measured first: any query of a table with a policy was 501, `CREATE VIEW … OPTIONS (privacy_policy)` 501. The policy is set by `CREATE TABLE`, `CREATE VIEW`, `ALTER TABLE` and `ALTER VIEW … SET OPTIONS (privacy_policy = '…')` (kept by the front with the table's creation time) and by `tables.insert`, `patch` and `update` of a view with `view.privacyPolicy` (the REST resource has it only on a view). The engine knows nothing of it: the front enforces it in its query rewrite, before anything runs. **Aggregation threshold** (`aggregation_threshold_policy`: `threshold`, `privacy_unit_column`): a statement that reads the table or view must be a `SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD [OPTIONS (threshold, privacy_unit_column)]` reading it in its own `FROM` clause, else **400 `invalidQuery`** ("You must use SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD for this query because a privacy policy is set on ds.v.", CloudBurrow's wording, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analysis-rules>)); (#1502) the clause is part of every SELECT's syntax, so that SELECT may be a parenthesized subquery, a CTE's query, the query after a `WITH` list or `CREATE TABLE … AS`'s query (the docs' rows from `SELECT * FROM (SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD …) WHERE n >= 3`, from a CTE, joined with another table, and written by `CREATE TABLE … AS`); (#1517) more than one per query, each rewritten in its place (two CTEs at thresholds 3 and 4 give P91 3 and U25 4 4; two scalar subqueries 3 and NULL), and one inside another is **400**, "a multi-level aggregation query" as the clause's reference says; it is sent on without the clause and with `HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT unit) >= threshold` (with no `GROUP BY`, one group of every row), so the docs' examples return their rows: threshold 3 gives P91 and U25, C83 (2 students) dropped; `OPTIONS (threshold = 4)` gives U25; 5 gives no rows. 400 too: a query threshold below the policy's, another `privacy_unit_column`, the privacy unit column projected (outside an aggregate) or `SELECT *`, an aggregate other than the clause's 13 (`APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT`, `AVG`, `COUNT`, `COUNTIF`, `LOGICAL_AND`, `LOGICAL_OR`, `SUM`, `COVAR_POP`, `COVAR_SAMP`, `STDDEV_POP`, `STDDEV_SAMP`, `VAR_POP`, `VAR_SAMP`), a nested aggregate, no aggregate, time travel (BigQuery disables it on such a view). The clause with both `OPTIONS` on tables with no policy is carried out the same way. A NULL privacy unit is not counted, which can only drop more groups (BigQuery's handling UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analysis-rules>)). Messages other than the documented ones are CloudBurrow's (UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analysis-rules>)). **Join restriction** (`join_restriction_policy`: `join_condition`, `join_allowed_columns`): the columns of the table or view that the `ON` or `USING` of the `INNER JOIN`s of its `FROM` clause name are checked: `JOIN_ALL` "Joining must occur on all of the following columns [test_score, last_name] on table ds.v.", `JOIN_ANY` "Joining must occur on at least one of the following columns […] on table ds.v.", `JOIN_NOT_REQUIRED` with no allowed column "At least one allowed column must be specified with join_condition = 'JOIN_NOT_REQUIRED'.", a join on another column or any join under `JOIN_BLOCKED` "Join occurring on a restricted column." (BigQuery's documented messages), all **400**; the allowed joins run. (#1502) A join restriction read inside a subquery's `SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD` is checked in that `FROM` clause (an aggregation threshold and `JOIN_ANY` view joined on test_score in a subquery gives U25 4). Joins that are not INNER follow each condition's documented wording: `JOIN_BLOCKED` "can't be joined along any column", so a `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`, `CROSS` or comma join is refused "Join occurring on a restricted column."; `JOIN_ALL`'s columns "must be inner joined upon", so a `LEFT JOIN` on them or a `CROSS JOIN` is refused "Joining must occur on all …"; `JOIN_NOT_REQUIRED` "If a join is used, only the columns in join_allowed_columns can be used", so a `LEFT JOIN` on an allowed column runs (11 rows), one on another column, a `CROSS` or comma join is refused "Join occurring on a restricted column."; `JOIN_ANY` with no allowed column joined upon by any join is refused "Joining must occur on at least one …". (#1517) `JOIN_ANY`'s "At least one column in join_allowed_columns must be joined upon" names no kind of join, so a `LEFT JOIN` upon an allowed column runs (11 rows, 5 matched; UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analysis-rules>): the list overlap rule's summary "Only overlapping rows can be queried after a join operation" is not measured against an outer join), and `JOIN_ALL` met by its `INNER JOIN` allows a `LEFT JOIN` alongside on allowed columns (UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analysis-rules>), by the same wording; a restricted column is still refused); a `NATURAL` join is **400** "Syntax error: Unexpected keyword NATURAL", as `NATURAL` is a reserved keyword (lexical#reserved_keywords) and the join operation has no NATURAL form (query-syntax#join_types). (#1517, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax>)) A query with no privacy clause at all that reads an aggregation threshold or differential privacy table or view in a subquery, a CTE, or through another view's query is **400** "You must use SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD (or DIFFERENTIAL_PRIVACY) for this query because a privacy policy is set on ds.v.", BigQuery's error for a read without the clause, the analysis rules saying only that such a view "can be queried with" the clause. **In a script** (#1502) that reads such a table or view, the script runs a statement at a time, each checked as a lone query in its turn: a `CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD` then a query of it with a `DECLARE`d variable gives U25 4; a statement without the clause is refused 400 after the statements before it ran, as BigQuery runs a script's statements in turn. **501**, never answered as if the table had no policy, as BigQuery documents none of them: in a query with a privacy clause, a read of it in a subquery or CTE other than in the `FROM` clause of its own `SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD` (`SELECT WITH AGGREGATION_THRESHOLD COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM v)`, a CTE of its rows read by the clause: the rows would leave the subquery not aggregated) or in another view's query (also through the emulator's inlined view text); a join restricted table in a subquery or CTE; a decorator, a script inside a transaction, a set operation, `QUALIFY`, `WINDOW`, an analytic function or a function called through a path (a UDF) in the clause, and `tabledata.list`, copy, extract, clone and Storage Read of it. **Differential privacy** (#1455, `internal/bigqueryfront/differentialprivacy.go`): `SELECT WITH DIFFERENTIAL_PRIVACY OPTIONS (epsilon, delta, max_groups_contributed, privacy_unit_column)` with the DP aggregate functions `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(x)`, `SUM`, `AVG` (each with `contribution_bounds_per_group => (lower, upper)` or implicit bounds) and `PERCENTILE_CONT(x, p, contribution_bounds_per_row => (lower, upper))`, a `GROUP BY`, a `WHERE`, and an `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT` of the noisy rows. The noise is real, from Google's own differential privacy library (`github.com/google/differential-privacy/go/v4` v4.1.0, Apache 2.0, pinned in go.mod, NOTICE): the front groups the rows by the `GROUP BY` and the privacy unit column in a query of its own, then bounds each unit's contributions (at most `max_groups_contributed` groups, a uniform sample, default 1, `NULL` no limit; each contribution clamped to the bounds: a unit's row count for `COUNT`, its sum for `SUM`, its average for `AVG`, as the reference's example gives pencil 40 and pen 18.5), splits epsilon as the reference says (n aggregates and the group selection each epsilon/(n+1), with l0 sensitivity `max_groups_contributed`), drops the groups whose Laplace-noised count of distinct privacy units is under the threshold the whole delta gives (the library's `Count.ThresholdedResult`), and adds Laplace noise: `COUNT` and an `INT64` `SUM` integer noise, a `FLOAT64` `SUM` float noise, `AVG` the library's `BoundedMean` of the units' averages, `PERCENTILE_CONT` its `BoundedQuantiles` (one sampled value per unit and group, CloudBurrow's choice, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/differential-privacy>)). Bounds not given are found from the data with half the aggregate's epsilon (a noisy histogram of powers of two, as the library's approximate bounds); with few privacy units this finds none and the query returns no rows ("Implicit bounding can fail with datasets that contain a low number of privacy units, returning no results"). A NULL privacy unit contributes nothing (UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/differential-privacy>)). Tested by the noise model's properties, not values: epsilon 1e20 gives the reference's rows exactly (pen 18.5, pencil 40, scissors 8; COUNT and SUM of the professors table); with epsilon 1 counts vary run to run around the true value within the Laplace spread (20 runs, distinct values, mean within 4 of 200); a group of one privacy unit is always dropped; contributions clamped (a sum of 150 per unit clamped to 10); `max_groups_contributed = 1` counts each unit in one group. **`differential_privacy_policy`** (`privacy_unit_column`, `max_epsilon_per_query`, `delta_per_query`, `epsilon_budget`, `delta_budget`, `max_groups_contributed`, with the ranges the analysis rules give, else the query is 501 with the reason): a query of the table or view must be a lone `SELECT WITH DIFFERENTIAL_PRIVACY`, else **400**; its options default to the policy's (epsilon `max_epsilon_per_query`, delta `delta_per_query`); **400** with BigQuery's documented messages for an epsilon above `max_epsilon_per_query` ("Epsilon is too high: 1e+20, policy for table ds.ExamView allows max 10.01") and once the queries' epsilon or delta would pass the budget ("Privacy budget is not sufficient for table 'ds.ExamView' in this query.", the third query of epsilon 10 against 25.6, as the example), and (CloudBurrow's wording, UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/differential-privacy>)) for a delta other than `delta_per_query`, another `privacy_unit_column`, and a `max_groups_contributed` above the policy's. The budget spent is kept by the front (`dpbudget.json` on its state directory) per view, its creation time and its policy, so `ALTER VIEW … SET OPTIONS (privacy_policy)` resets it, as documented. Refused **400** too, as the reference says (wording UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/differential-privacy>)): an aggregate other than the four (`MAX`), no privacy unit column, `PERCENTILE_CONT` without bounds, a multi-level aggregation, `SELECT *`. **#1482**: **`HAVING`** applies to the noisy rows, by an alias or a grouping column (`HAVING n > 1`), by the select list's DP aggregate call written again (`HAVING COUNT(*, …) = 1`, matched token by token, any case), or by a DP aggregate only `HAVING` calls, a hidden aggregate of the query that takes its share of the epsilon (epsilon/(n+1) with it counted, query-syntax#dp_epsilon) and is not a column of the result; measured without noise on the reference's professors (`HAVING n > 1` pen 3, pencil 4; `HAVING SUM(…) > 50 AND item != 'pencil'` pen 3, two columns). The clause **in parentheses**, a subquery's or a CTE's query (`SELECT … FROM (SELECT WITH DIFFERENTIAL_PRIVACY …)`, `WITH d AS (SELECT WITH DIFFERENTIAL_PRIVACY …) SELECT SUM(s) …`), is carried out first and its noisy rows take its place, so the outer query reads them (a CTE total of 210 over 3 groups; with epsilon 1, ten noisy counts within 40 of 200, varying); a table with a `differential_privacy_policy` may be read in its FROM clause. **In a script** each such statement runs in its turn, a statement at a time, so it reads what earlier statements wrote and the script's variables (a `CREATE TABLE`, an `INSERT` and `WHERE quantity >= least`, `least` a `DECLARE`d variable), its noise drawn and its budget charged once (a script of two queries of epsilon 10 against 25.6, then a third refused and one of 5 not; the script's last query, answered again as the client's request, keeps its child job's rows). **`group_selection_strategy`** `LAPLACE_THRESHOLD` (the default) or **`PUBLIC_GROUPS`**, as GoogleSQL's reference documents it (query-syntax#dp_group_selection_strategy; BigQuery's own clause lists only epsilon, delta, max_groups_contributed and privacy_unit_column, so BigQuery's acceptance of it is UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax>)): the groups are not selected (no noisy unit count, no threshold, the epsilon split among the aggregates only, delta may be 0), so each group of the public group join is kept, one of a single unit and one of none too (its aggregates of no contribution, a COUNT about 0), and a private group not in the public table is not (the reference's example: book 0, pen 3, pencil 4, no scissors; with epsilon 1, six runs of `big`, `none` and `small` all kept, within 20 of 200, 0 and 1). It must have a public group join for every grouping item, a `LEFT [OUTER] JOIN` or `RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN` whose public side is a `SELECT DISTINCT` subquery, joined `USING` or `ON` each grouping item, else **400** (CloudBurrow's wording). Units `TestDPHaving`, `TestDPPublicGroups`. **#1517 (UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/differential-privacy>))**: an expression over DP aggregates in the select list (`ROUND(SUM(…) / COUNT(…), 2) AS per_row`, `COUNT(…) + 1 plus`), which neither reference documents, follows what both document of `HAVING`: each call is one more aggregate, a hidden one taking its share of the epsilon (query-syntax#dp_epsilon), and the expression is evaluated on the noisy values (post-processing keeps them differentially private); measured without noise on the professors (pen 19.33 4, pencil 36 5, `HAVING per_row > 10` by its alias), and with a policy view the expression is its count's noisy value times ten, the query's epsilon is charged once (two queries of 10 against a budget of 25, the third refused "Privacy budget is not sufficient …"), `max_groups_contributed` 1 of the policy bounds each student to one group, and a DP aggregate inside another is still **400** multi-level. Unit `TestDPExpressionItem`. **501**: `COUNT(DISTINCT …)` and the option `max_rows_contributed`, which neither BigQuery's reference (query-syntax#dp_clause lists only epsilon, delta, max_groups_contributed and privacy_unit_column; aggregate-dp-functions gives `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(expression)` only) nor GoogleSQL's documents for differential privacy (read again for #1517 and on 2026-11-18 for #1589), and the `report_format => 'JSON' | 'PROTO'` argument of `AVG`, `COUNT` and `SUM`, which GoogleSQL's aggregate-dp-functions documents (since 2026-10-20) but BigQuery's does not (unit `TestParseDPQuery`, compat `TestBigQueryDifferentialPrivacyMore`; #1589); the clause with a set operation, `QUALIFY`, `WINDOW`, `GROUP BY ROLLUP`, the deprecated `ANON_*` functions, a query of two tables with a `differential_privacy_policy`, the clause inside another differentially private query or not in parentheses (after `UNION ALL`), and in a script inside a transaction. Not done: a DP subquery of a CTE that reads an earlier CTE of the same `WITH` (it is carried out alone, and fails as the engine finds no such table). Units `TestRewriteAggregationThreshold`, `TestCheckJoinRestriction`, `TestParsePrivacyPolicy`, `TestPrivacyViewOfPolicyView`, `TestPrivacySubqueries`, `TestParseDPQuery`, `TestDPComputeWithoutNoise`, `TestDPNoiseDistribution`, `TestDPMaxGroupsContributed`, `TestDPImplicitBounds`, `TestParseDPPolicyAndBudget`. https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/analysis-rules, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#agg_threshold_clause, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#dp_clause, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/aggregate-dp-functions |

| Streaming buffer of a partitioned table (`tabledata.insertAll`) | **Verified** (#1273): a streamed row reads `_PARTITIONTIME` and `_PARTITIONDATE` NULL and is in `$__UNPARTITIONED__` while it is in the streaming buffer, as BigQuery documents ("Recently streamed rows to an ingestion time partitioned table temporarily have a NULL value for the `_PARTITIONTIME` pseudocolumn"); `tables.get` answers `streamingBuffer` (`estimatedRows`, `oldestEntryTime`; no `estimatedBytes`) and `numRows` without the buffered rows; a copy job does not copy them. The buffer flushes in the background, 20 seconds after its oldest row (BigQuery gives "typically a few minutes" and no SLA), and the rows then read their partition's time. A Storage Write API row is not buffered: it reads its partition's time at once, and DML changes it, as BigQuery documents for the Write API's rows ("recent writes" through the gRPC Storage Write API can be modified with `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `MERGE`, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/updating-data; https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/write-api documents no `streamingBuffer`). Since the last of #1273 (`TestBigQueryColumnStreamingBuffer`), a table partitioned by a column or an integer range has a streaming buffer too, as BigQuery documents ("When you stream data to a time-partitioned table, each partition has a streaming buffer"): a streamed row is read by queries at once; a time-unit column table's goes to `$__UNPARTITIONED__` ("initially placed in the `__UNPARTITIONED__` partition"), but a daily table's whose day is from 7 days ago to 3 days ahead stays in its own partition ("only data outside of the date range (last 7 days to future 3 days) is extracted to the UNPARTITIONED partition"), and a value more than 10 years back or 1 year ahead is rejected, an `insertErrors` entry `invalid` (wording UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/streaming-data-into-bigquery>)); an integer-range table's goes to `$__UNPARTITIONED__` (BigQuery documents nothing else for it); `tables.get` answers `streamingBuffer` and `numRows` without the rows, a copy leaves them out, and the buffer flushes as above. Since #1370 a streamed row stays unmodifiable for BigQuery's 30 minutes ("the recent writes are those that occurred within the last 30 minutes"), not until the flush: next row. A table kept in an instance's state from before the engine had the column gets it when the instance next starts, NULL on its old rows, whose stream times were never recorded (googlesqlite patch 0089, #1458: the engine's regression test `TestStreamedAtColumnOfAnOlderTable` ages a saved table and reopens it; no client can make such a table, so no compat test), and the rows streamed to it from then on are held for 30 minutes. **Not implemented**: a row written by the gRPC Storage Write API is not held (BigQuery documents it modifiable, row above) | `TestBigQueryDMLOfRecentlyStreamedRows`, `TestBigQueryColumnStreamingBuffer` (#1370), `TestBigQueryStreamTimeOfEveryTable`, `TestBigQueryStreamTimeOfMadeTables` (#1458), official Go client (`Inserter().Put`, `Query`, `Table.Metadata`, `CopierFrom`, `LoaderFrom`). Measured first: DML changed a streamed row of a table that is not partitioned at once. Every table made by `tables.insert` or a `CREATE TABLE` with a column list (not `TEMP`) has the engine pseudo-column `_PARTITION_STREAMED TIMESTAMP` (googlesqlite patch 0030, bigquery-emulator patch 0018), left out of its schema, of `SELECT *` and of `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS`; every `insertAll` of a table (not a view, not a `templateSuffix` or partition-decorator stream) gives its rows their stream time, as a partitioned table's does (the engine's `insertAll` writes it, bigquery-emulator patch 0081, #1624; a row of a table partitioned by a column whose value the front cannot read as a time still goes through a scratch table). The front keeps each table's last stream time in its state directory (`streambuffers-recent.json`) and counts the rows a statement would change among those streamed within 30 minutes of its clock (`internal/bigqueryfront/streamingbuffer.go`). The clock is the BigQuery front's, one for the whole instance: the CloudBurrow extension `POST /cloudburrow/bigquery/v2/clock:advance` with `{"seconds": n}` (n not negative; it answers `{"time": …}`) moves it forward for every table and dataset, which also flushes every streaming buffer whose 20 seconds have passed by then, and the clock does not move back until the instance restarts (a stream time kept under an advanced clock is kept as it was) |

| Change history: `APPENDS(TABLE t, start, end)` and `CHANGES(TABLE t, start, end)`, `_CHANGE_TYPE`, `_CHANGE_TIMESTAMP`, `_CHANGE_IS_FOR_UPDATE`, `enable_change_history` | **Verified** (#1418) through `jobs.query` and `jobs.insert`, for rows written by DML (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE`, `TRUNCATE TABLE`), `tabledata.insertAll`, load jobs (`WRITE_APPEND`, and `WRITE_TRUNCATE`, whose replaced rows are `DELETE`s), the Storage Write API (default stream) and a query's destination table, `enable_change_history` set by `CREATE TABLE … OPTIONS` or `ALTER TABLE … SET OPTIONS`; the documented refusals, 400 (wording UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/change-history>)): `CHANGES` of a table without `enable_change_history = TRUE`, a start before the dataset's time travel window (`maxTimeTravelHours`, 168 by default) or a NULL start of a table made before it, a future end, either function on a view, a materialized view or a snapshot, either function inside a multi-statement transaction, `CHANGES` of a table with change data capture (a primary key and `max_staleness`, the configuration BigQuery's CDC uses; the upserts themselves since #1999, row *Storage Write API: change data capture*), and a `CHANGES` range over one day as given (all tested, #1466); a range over one day from a NULL start (the table's creation) is refused by the same check, untested (no test table is a day old: creation and change times follow the instance clock (#1487), which can be advanced a day, but every later test on the instance would then run a day ahead); a start before the table's creation reads from its creation, a NULL end is the query's start. Since #1522: a table with a column whose name starts `_CHANGE_` keeps its history (`TestBigQueryChangeHistoryOfChangeNamedColumns`, googlesqlite patch 0063): BigQuery reserves only the prefixes `_CHANGE_SEQUENCE_NUMBER`, `_CHANGE_TYPE` and `_CHANGE_TIMESTAMP` ([column names](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/schemas)), which `tables.insert` refuses 400, so another, `_CHANGE_NOTE` say, is the table's own; and `ALTER SCHEMA … SET OPTIONS (max_time_travel_hours = …)` lets go of the history outside the old window first, as `datasets.patch` does (`TestBigQueryAlterSchemaTimeTravelLetsGoFirst`, the row of `ALTER SCHEMA`). **Partial**: a table with a column named `_CHANGE_IS_FOR_UPDATE` (a name BigQuery does not reserve, but the change table's own) keeps no history; a transaction committed by an `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` of `COMMIT` is 501, as every transaction statement an `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` runs; `enable_change_history` is no field of the REST `Table` resource (google.golang.org/api v0.298.0's discovery document has none), so `tables.insert` and `tables.patch` cannot set it, as in BigQuery. The ten-minute lag from `end` to now that older documentation gave `CHANGES` is not in the documentation read 2026-10-16 ("If the `end_timestamp` value is `NULL`, all changes made up to the start time of the query are included"), so there is none | `TestBigQueryChangeHistory` (BigQuery's documented `CHANGES` example, its rows and one `_CHANGE_TIMESTAMP` per statement, and `APPENDS` after `ADD COLUMN`), `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryWritePaths` (`Inserter.Put`: `tabledata.insertAll`; `Loader` `WRITE_APPEND` and `WRITE_TRUNCATE`; `managedwriter` default stream; `Query` with `Dst`; `MERGE`; `TRUNCATE TABLE`), `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryRefusals`, `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryRebuilds`, `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryReplace`, `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryLimits` (#1466: the refusals, and `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` after `clock:advance`), `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryCommittedTransaction`, `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryRetention` (#1503: a 48-hour dataset, the clock advanced 49 hours, the window made 168 hours), `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryOfChangeNamedColumns` and `TestBigQueryAlterSchemaTimeTravelLetsGoFirst` (#1522), unit `TestCommittedTransactionsAreKept`, official Go client. Measured first: `APPENDS(TABLE t, NULL, NULL)` failed 400 in the engine, which kept no history of a table (`FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` reads only now, #1276). Design: the engine records every change (googlesqlite patch 0036): each `project.dataset.table` a `CREATE TABLE` makes gets a change table, `table$changes`, of its columns and the three change columns, filled by SQLite triggers `AFTER INSERT`, `DELETE` and `UPDATE` (an update is a `DELETE` with `_CHANGE_IS_FOR_UPDATE` of the old row and an `UPDATE` of the new), so every write path is recorded where it lands, not path by path in the front; the change time is the time of the transaction's first change, the same for all its rows; an update of a row the same transaction inserted (the emulator's NUMERIC rounding triggers) is part of the INSERT; a wildcard and INFORMATION_SCHEMA leave change tables out. The front (`internal/bigqueryfront/changehistory.go`) checks each call as BigQuery documents it and writes it as a subquery of the change table's window, the job keeping the client's statement. Costs: every row written to any table (but the front's own `_cloudburrow…` datasets) is written twice (APPENDS reads any table, and the option can be set later), a `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE TABLE` or `WRITE_TRUNCATE` copies every row it deletes, each change costs an indexed prune of changes older than seven days, and the change tables live in the engine's database, so persistent mode keeps them. Measured (#1466, the engine alone, 50,000 rows of three columns inserted, 10,000 updated, 10,000 deleted, in a file database): inserts took the same time with and without the history (3.4 s, the statements' analysis dominates), the `UPDATE` 118 ms against 32 ms and the `DELETE` 64 ms against 22 ms, and the database was 25.7 MB against 5.5 MB (the change rows and their two indexes). It is not reduced: BigQuery's `APPENDS` and `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` read any table within its time travel window, whatever its options ("Setting a table's enable_change_history option to FALSE does not reduce the data processed by APPENDS"), so recording only once a table has `enable_change_history`, or is first read with `APPENDS`, would leave those reads without the rows before; only `CHANGES`'s `DELETE` and `UPDATE` records could wait for the option (the documentation warns history before it "might be incomplete"), but time travel reads them too. Rebuilds and replaces (#1466, `internal/bigqueryfront/changehistorycarry.go`): the front copies the old change table aside before it deletes the table, and carries it into the new one, the copied rows' `INSERT`s marked `CARRY` and each old row ended by an `END` (both left out of `APPENDS` and `CHANGES`; a replace's are `INSERT` and `DELETE`), the old rows' identities moved below every rowid, the old `START` row kept. A table with a column of its own named `_CHANGE_IS_FOR_UPDATE` (made by `tables.insert` or DDL; BigQuery reserves only the prefixes `_CHANGE_TYPE`, `_CHANGE_TIMESTAMP` and `_CHANGE_SEQUENCE_NUMBER`) keeps its history like any table, through an `ALTER TABLE` that makes it again too: the change table's own flag is `_CHANGE_TYPE_FOR_UPDATE`, under a reserved prefix, and a change table made before is renamed to it when the engine opens its database (#1548, `TestBigQueryChangeHistoryForUpdateColumn`; engine `TestChangeHistoryUpdateFlag`, googlesqlite patch 0065). CHANGES of such a table has two columns of that name, the table's and the flag, so it reads the table's other columns and `_CHANGE_TYPE` by name; what BigQuery does there is not documented. Every regular table keeps a history, as `APPENDS` and time travel read any table's, but not a second copy of its rows (#1597, googlesqlite patch 0074): the record of a row inserted, or of an `UPDATE`'s new row, keeps no values while the row is unchanged in the table; the next change of the row writes its old values in, and a read of the history (`APPENDS`, `CHANGES`, time travel, undelete, a rebuild) reads the pending ones from the table first. Measured on the engine alone (50,000 rows, 10,000 updated, 10,000 deleted): the same insert time, the database 39.7 MB instead of 51.9 (16.3 with no history), an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` a fifth to two fifths slower. Engine regression tests `TestChangeHistory` (googlesqlite patch 0036), `TestChangeHistoryReplace` (patch 0044), `TestChangeHistoryPending` (patch 0074); unit `TestChangeFuncs`, `TestChangesInTransaction`. https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/change-history, https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/time-series-functions |

Read back: a query job with a label, `QUERY`, `SELECT`, `DONE`, its text and label, `creation_time` within the hour; an `INSERT` job with `dml_statistics.inserted_row_count` 2; a failed query with its `error_result`; `JOBS_BY_USER` the same jobs (an instance has one user). `query_dialect` is `GOOGLE_SQL` or `LEGACY_SQL` for a job that asked one, and for one that asked none `DEFAULT_LEGACY_SQL`, or `DEFAULT_GOOGLE_SQL` when its region's `default_sql_dialect_option` made GoogleSQL the default at `jobs.insert` (the [JOBS page](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/information-schema-jobs)' four values, read 2026-10-17; #1595, `TestBigQueryJobsQueryDialect`; a `jobs.query` that asks none is `DEFAULT_LEGACY_SQL`, and the record is not kept across restarts). Since #1201 the rows are written as array literals of at most 100 elements joined by `UNION ALL`: one literal of every job failed 400 "too many arguments on function googlesqlite_make_array" on an instance of 1,630 jobs (measured, after the whole `TestBigQuery*` suite), as the engine's array is a SQLite function of one argument per element (unit `TestRowsSubqueryArraysAreCapped`); the other views the front writes with the same helper (`rowsSubquery`) are split the same way. Since #1369 the engine lists jobs in one SQLite scan (patch bigquery-emulator 0017: `jobs.list` of 5,000 jobs 8.7 s to 0.09 s), and the front keeps only the jobs that can pass the query's filters before writing rows (`infoschemajobsfilter.go`): in the top-level `WHERE` of the one `SELECT` whose only `FROM` item is the view, a conjunct at a time, `job_id`, `state`, `job_type`, `project_id` and `parent_job_id` `=` or `IN` string literals, `parent_job_id IS [NOT] NULL`, and `creation_time` against a `TIMESTAMP` literal or (lower bound, a minute early) `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` less an `INTERVAL`; and `ORDER BY creation_time [ASC|DESC] LIMIT n [OFFSET m]` when the whole `WHERE` was read and the select list aggregates nothing. The query still runs with its `WHERE`, so the answer is the same. Measured at 5,000 jobs: `WHERE job_id = ...` 54 s to 0.24 s, `ORDER BY creation_time DESC LIMIT 3` 0.21 s; a query with no filter the front reads (`SELECT COUNT(*)`) 54 s to 13 s, still growing with the jobs (#1369; a table of the rows since #1378, written as the jobs are made since #1419, below). No job count reaches a cap of SQLite (#1374): the rows are array literals of at most 100 (#1201) in `UNION ALL`s of at most 100 terms, nested past that (SQLite caps a compound `SELECT` at 500); the whole `TestBigQuery*` suite twice on one instance passes. Since #1378 a query with no filter the front reads reads a table of the rows the front keeps in its hidden dataset (`_cloudburrow_query_results.cloudburrow_information_schema_jobs`, `jobstable.go`), to which before each such query it writes only the rows new or changed since the last and deletes those of jobs gone; it is made again when the front starts, forgotten when the emulator restarts, and left out of the dataset views. Measured at 5,000 jobs (`--services bigquery,storage`, through the front): `SELECT COUNT(*)` 24.0 s the first time and 7.1–7.6 s after, to 29.1 s the first time (the table is written) and 1.4–1.5 s after; the answer is the literal's (measured at 122 jobs: the same rows, by a hash of 21 columns of every row, as a query filtered by `project_id`, which reads the literal). Since #1419 the engine lists each job with its configuration when asked for `projection=full` (patch bigquery-emulator 0022), so a list sends no `jobs.get` (the first list of 5,000 `jobs.query` jobs took 16.6 s of them), a list gives each job the configuration it read even past the 20,000 the front keeps (past 5,000, the cap before, some were listed with none, so their rows had a `NULL` `job_type` and `query`), and once a project's table is made the front writes it in the background a second after each job made through it, so a query writes only the last second's rows. Measured at 5,000 jobs made by 16 clients at once (`--services bigquery,storage`, arm64, through the front, `TestBigQueryInformationSchemaJobsAtScale`): the first `SELECT COUNT(*)` after them 25.1 s to 0.41 s, the ones after 0.24–0.27 s to 0.28–0.36 s, an unfiltered `GROUP BY state, job_type` 0.33 s; making the jobs 32 s to 48 s (the background writes); the answer is the literal's (at 5,006 jobs: the same count and fingerprint of 22 columns of every row as a query filtered by `project_id`). Since #1515 a filtered query that keeps more than 100 jobs reads the table too, its `WHERE` run by the engine (a literal costs the engine about 2 ms a row): measured at 2,100 `jobs.query` jobs (`--services bigquery,storage`, arm64, through the front), `TestBigQueryIngestionPartitionHistory`'s `GROUP BY` of the nine statistics columns `WHERE job_type = 'QUERY'` 4.1–4.7 s to 0.14 s (4.7 s the first time after the front starts, when the table is written), `COUNT(*) WHERE job_type = 'QUERY'` 4.0–4.8 s to 0.12 s, and an unfiltered `COUNT(*)` and `SELECT * ... LIMIT 10`, which read the table before too, 0.22–0.49 s before and 0.12 s after (unit `TestJobsTableReadByFilteredQueries`). Since #1564 a filtered query reads the table as soon as it is made, whatever it keeps, and a sync of it costs what the jobs changed since the last do: the engine lists the jobs after the cursor by its job order's keys (bigquery-emulator patch 0060), where it had read every job first. Measured with the kind node at two CPUs, the `COUNT(*)`s after the first took 0.04 s at 5,000 and 10,000 jobs and 0.06–0.14 s at 20,000 (0.10–0.17 s, 0.17 s and 0.31–0.59 s before), the first after a burst 0.15, 0.25 and 0.31 s (0.25, 0.37 and 1.57 s), and one `WHERE creation_time` of the last minute 0.04–0.07 s (0.58, 1.02 and 2.26 s). Since #1639 the `jobs.list` path decodes the engine's list once, each layer changing it in place, where each layer decoded and wrote it again, and the job references of a jobs answer are given their location without decoding the rest of it (a query's rows); since #1633 a query that names its jobs (`job_id` `=` or `IN`) before the table is made lists those and the jobs the engine made since the newest it listed (bigquery-emulator patch 0064), not every job, and its filter cuts them as before, so the rows are the same. Measured at 10,000 jobs in the pod (`--services storage,bigquery`, arm64, 2026-10-19, after the `TestBigQuery*` suite): 20 `WHERE job_id = ...` queries 0.39 s each to 0.016 s, 227 MB allocated by the front each to 4.4 MB; 20 `WHERE job_type = 'LOAD'` (every job listed) 0.39 s to 0.21 s, 233 MB to 58 MB; the front's peak RSS over `TestBigQueryInformationSchemaJobs -count=3` 305 MB to 173 MB (its `GOMEMLIMIT` is 256 MiB), 5.2 GB allocated to 0.7 GB; a `jobs.list` page of 50 0.20 s either way. Since #1633 too, before the table is made, a query that keeps only jobs not `DONE` (`state` `=` or `IN` without `'DONE'`) lists the jobs the front keeps of those the engine listed not `DONE`, and those the engine made after the newest it listed then (`jobsopen.go`): every list of the engine's jobs brings what is kept up to date (a list of every job, a client's `jobs.list` too, makes it anew), it is kept in the front's state directory, and it is forgotten when the emulator restarts or the project is purged, the next query then listing every job; a cursor the engine has no job of, or another job of (the emulator restarted while the front was down), lists every job too. A query that keeps the children of some jobs (`parent_job_id` `=` or `IN`) lists the children the front recorded of them (the row *A script's child jobs*), which alone have a `parent_job_id`, and the jobs made since the newest listed. Either way the filter cuts them as it cuts a list of every job, so the rows are the same. A `job_type` filter still lists every job until the table is made: neither the engine nor the front keeps an index of a job's type, and nearly every job is a query, so one would cut little. Measured at 10,000 jobs in the pod (`--services storage,bigquery`, arm64, 2026-10-19, through the official Go client): `WHERE state = 'RUNNING'` 0.21–0.26 s before (every job listed, on an instance of 10,000 `SELECT 1` jobs) and 0.02–0.03 s after its first (0.17 s, every job listed once; on an instance of the `TestBigQuery*` suite's 2,703 jobs and 7,297 `SELECT 1` jobs, where `WHERE job_type = 'LOAD'`, which still lists every job, took 0.36–0.51 s), and `WHERE parent_job_id = 'nosuchjob'` 0.19–0.21 s to 0.02–0.03 s. BigQuery runs a multi-statement query as a parent job of `statementType` `SCRIPT`, "and each statement in the script creates a child job" ([multi-statement queries](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/multi-statement-queries), [ScriptStatistics](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/Job#ScriptStatistics)). The front's run of a script (`internal/bigqueryfront/scriptflow.go`) sends each statement, and each expression it evaluates (a `DECLARE`'s `DEFAULT`, a `SET`'s value, a condition, a `FOR`'s query), as a job of its own on the emulator; once the parent is answered, each is recorded as its child (`internal/bigqueryfront/scriptjobs.go`): `statistics.parentJobId`, `scriptStatistics.evaluationKind` (`STATEMENT` or `EXPRESSION`) and its `stackFrames`. Since #1569 every child's frames are where its statement or expression is written, read as the script runs rather than by searching the script for the text it sent: the 1-based `startLine`, `startColumn`, `endLine` and `endColumn` (its last character) and its `text` as written, with its variables' names, so a statement that reads a variable, the last statement and a statement written twice each have their own; a statement `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` runs, and the expressions it evaluates, are at that `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`; an expression's frame is the expression alone (a `DECLARE`'s `DEFAULT`, a condition, a `CALL` argument; BigQuery's frame of an expression UNVERIFIED (docs re-read 2026-10-17: <https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/rest/v2/Job>)); a statement of a `CALL`ed procedure has a frame in the procedure's body (positions in the body from its `BEGIN`: the Job reference's `ScriptStackFrame` says "all line/column numbers are relative to the procedure body") with `procedureId` `project.dataset.name`, then the `CALL`'s, innermost first. Read back (`TestBigQueryScriptChildFrames`), for a script of 23 lines: the `DECLARE`'s `DEFAULT` at 1:25, the `CREATE TABLE`, statements reading a variable inside `BEGIN` and an `EXCEPTION` handler, the `IF`'s condition, the failed `SELECT` inside the `IF`, an `INSERT` in a `LOOP`, the procedure's `INSERT` (frames: 2:3 in the procedure, then the `CALL` at 19:1), a child of the transaction and the last statement, a `DELETE` reading a variable, each at its line and column, and no child without a position; the console's read-write editor numbers each DML statement's sentence by it, the last one's too (`TestBigQueryReadWriteEditorThroughTheForms`); the parent has `numChildJobs` and `statementType` `SCRIPT`, in `jobs.insert`'s answer, `jobs.get` and `jobs.list`. The last statement, when a query, is run once more as a child of its own. Read back, for a script of a `DECLARE … DEFAULT`, a `CREATE TABLE`, an `IF` holding an `INSERT` and a `SELECT`: five children (three `STATEMENT`, two `EXPRESSION`), the `CREATE TABLE` frame at 2:1, the `INSERT` child with `numDmlAffectedRows` 2, `Job.Read` of the parent the `SELECT`'s rows, no child in the top-level `jobs.list`, and five rows of `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS` with the parent's `parent_job_id`. A child's `statementType` is the emulator's, `SELECT` for a DDL statement (#698). Since #1201 a statement that fails is a child job too, also when an `EXCEPTION` handler catches it (`TestBigQueryScriptFailedChildJobs`): measured first, it had none, as the emulator records no job for a `jobs.query` that fails; the front now makes one, a query job of a statement that does nothing, shown with the statement's text, failed with its error (`status.errorResult`) and with `parentJobId`, `evaluationKind` `STATEMENT` and the statement's stack frame (read back: the failed `SELECT` at 3:3, its error naming the missing table, its query the statement; the script's job failed with the `RAISE` no handler caught; a `RAISE`'s message is an `EXPRESSION` child). The children are in the front's memory (the last 5000), not its state directory. |

scriptdryrun.go); **Not implemented** (501): an `ALTER TABLE` or other statement the front carries out itself in a dry run of a script, a `TEMP` table in a transaction's script beyond row `Multi-statement transactions`, and what the statement is refused alone | `TestBigQueryStatementsInTempScripts`, `TestBigQueryTempScriptsInTurn`, `TestBigQueryStatementsLaterInAScript` and `TestBigQueryEveryScriptInTurn` (#1459), official Go client (`Query.Read`, `Query.Run`, `Job.Children`, `Client.JobFromID`, `Table.Metadata`, `Dataset.Metadata`). Measured first: each script was 501 notImplemented, nothing run. BigQuery keeps a `TEMP` table for the script and runs each statement as a child job ([multi-statement queries](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/multi-statement-queries#temporary_tables)). A `TEMP` table or function lasts only for the engine request that made it, so a script with one that the front would carry out a statement at a time (control flow, an `ALTER TABLE`, a query before its last statement, an `ASSERT`, `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`, `@@row_count`, `OPTIONS`), or that the emulator refuses as written but whose statements it runs alone, is run as #1434 runs a materialized view's (`internal/bigqueryfront/tempsession.go`): each `TEMP` table a table of the hidden results dataset for the script's length (and each `TEMP` function a function there), each name of it after the statement that makes it its path, also in an `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`'s statement, and that text carried out by the front a statement at a time, each a child job whose text names the script's own names; once it ends, failed or not, they are deleted. A script with no `TEMP` table that `checkDDL` refuses 501 as a whole, but none of whose statements it refuses alone (`splitCures`, `internal/bigqueryfront/scriptflow.go`), is carried out a statement at a time too, each statement as it is run on its own (a lone `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE`, `LIKE`/`COPY`/`CLONE`, `MERGE` from a subquery); an `ALTER TABLE` the front carries out itself is not a child job. And every other script of several statements with no `TEMP` table or function, which the emulator ran whole (no child jobs, rolled back whole through `jobs.query` when it failed, and 501 for what it refuses later in a script), is carried out a statement at a time too (`internal/bigqueryfront/dml.go`), as BigQuery runs a script: a query job that fails at a statement BigQuery fails `duplicate` or `resourceInUse` keeps that reason. A script's last statement keeps its place: a query is run once more as a child, a DML statement is the parent job (row `A script's child jobs`). Read back: the `ALTER TABLE`'s column, the `LIKE` table's schema, the replaced table's and the merged rows, the `TEMP` table gone after the script, the rows an `INSERT` before a failed statement kept and the one after it not run, and the child jobs' texts. Unit `TestTempSessionScript`, `TestReplacingATempTableIs501`, `TestEarlierQuery`, `TestScriptsCarriedOutInTurn`. |

One in an `EXCEPTION` block runs at once, to see its failure, and a query job ending in such a DML statement is recorded with a statement that does nothing. Every statement is checked before anything runs, whether or not its branch would run, and a name BigQuery refuses is **400** first: `` CREATE TABLE ds.`if!` `` in an `IF`, `` `loop!` `` in a `LOOP`, `` `handler!` `` in an `EXCEPTION` handler, and nothing is made (unit `TestDDLInBlocksAndAlterTable`). A loop that never ends fails after 24 hours, BigQuery's cumulative limit, or stops when the client's request is gone (units `TestScriptTimeLimit`, `TestScriptVariableLimits`, `TestScriptLastStatement`).
